11. Final independent conclusion
The documentary record is sufficient to establish that multiple Australian administrative and oversight processes affected access to complaint pathways, information, financial administration, disability support and representation.
It establishes more than the mere existence of allegations.
It establishes actual decisions, formal restrictions, statutory exclusions, administrative classifications and identifiable discrepancies in the documentary record.
Those facts justify an independent academic examination of administrative annihilation as a cumulative-effects construct.
The evidence also justifies the use of institutional fragmentation, administrative attrition, dependency and the paradox of protection as analytical categories.
The distinction between a decision and its consequences must remain central.
An institution may have statutory authority to make a decision. That does not make the decision immune from examination.
An institution may have a lawful reason to decline jurisdiction. That does not establish that the underlying concern was investigated elsewhere.
An institution may approve a funding plan. That does not establish that the funded assistance was delivered.
An institution may restrict correspondence. That does not answer whether the restriction left an effective avenue for raising new matters.
These are legitimate independent findings about institutional conduct and administrative consequences.
No official’s agreement is required to identify an inconsistency in an official document. No tribunal’s permission is required to compare two administrative decisions. No government determination is required to establish what an authentic letter says.
Equally, the evidence must be permitted to establish the limits of a conclusion, rather than being forced to support a predetermined outcome.
The appropriate academic conclusion is that the archive provides a substantial and identifiable documentary foundation for investigating cumulative administrative harm, institutional fragmentation and the erosion of practical civil participation.
It does not yet establish every alleged act, every technique or a coordinated criminal conspiracy.
That is the distinction between an evidentiary finding and an unsupported accusation.
The research does not need institutional permission to examine institutional power.

On 27 March 2023, the Federal Court of Australia’s General Counsel, acting as an authorised officer under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 2013, recorded that the disclosure concerned conduct falling within categories including perverting the course of justice, maladministration and danger to health or safety. THE WHISTLEBLOWER, THE WITNESS AND THE STATE
Barran Dodger: An Independent Historical, Documentary and International Comparative Examination of Truth-Telling, Institutional Power, Alleged Persecution, Corruption, Administrative Erasure and Accountability
Commissioned research report — reconstructed from the beginning
Research principle: Preservation First. Examination Second. Conclusion Last.
Standard of presentation: Documented Fact · Official Record · Author Allegation · Evidentiary Inference · Unverified Matter.
Guiding proposition: Time is the witness. Truth is the judge.
PART I — PURPOSE, SCOPE AND EVIDENTIARY FOUNDATION
1. Executive purpose
This report examines the documentary record assembled by Barran Dodger, also known in the records and correspondence as Richard William McLean. It considers his public-interest disclosures, dealings with government agencies and oversight bodies, complaints concerning institutional conduct, requests for protection, and allegations of administrative, financial, legal and personal harm.
It asks a central historical and institutional question:
What does the accumulated documentary record show about the treatment of a person who repeatedly sought assistance, accountability and protection from institutions whose conduct he was questioning?
The report does not begin with the presumption that every allegation is true. Equally, it does not begin with the presumption that government institutions acted properly, that official correspondence is inherently reliable, or that an allegation becomes unworthy of examination because no authority has issued a final ruling.
It begins with the records.
Those records must be examined cumulatively. A letter cannot be understood only by reading its final paragraph. A refusal cannot be assessed without examining what was requested, what information was provided, what the institution acknowledged, what it declined to do, whether it identified an alternative pathway, and what happened after the refusal. A series of institutional responses cannot be treated as unrelated administrative events if the chronology, communications and consequences disclose a possible pattern.
The purpose is therefore not simply to recount a personal grievance. It is to examine a documentary history involving:
	•	Public-interest disclosure and whistleblower protections.
	•	Allegations of maladministration, corruption and perversion of the course of justice.
	•	Alleged institutional complicity, coordination, obstruction or retaliation.
	•	The treatment of complaints and requests for independent investigation.
	•	The consequences of repeated non-action, referrals, exclusions and refusals.
	•	Financial and administrative restrictions affecting independence and access to resources.
	•	Disability, housing, safety, support and the practical consequences of institutional decisions.
	•	Documentary preservation, public access, chronology and evidentiary integrity.
	•	The historical comparison of whistleblowers, dissenters and people alleging institutional persecution.
	•	The remedies, accountability mechanisms and independent scrutiny that the record may warrant.
2. The governing evidentiary principle
The absence of an official determination is not proof that the alleged conduct did not occur.
An official determination can be important evidence. It is not the only form of evidence. Primary documents, contemporaneous correspondence, statutory notices, recorded decisions, financial records, medical records, witness accounts, metadata, audit trails and independently verifiable communications may establish facts without a later authority issuing a declaration about them.
For this report, the following distinctions apply:
Classification	Meaning
Documented fact	A fact directly established by an identifiable record or independently verifiable source
Official record	A document created or issued by a government body, court, statutory authority or other institution
Official acknowledgment	A statement in an official record acknowledging that a matter was raised, received, considered or acted upon
Author allegation	A claim made by Barran Dodger that requires examination against the available evidence
Evidentiary inference	A conclusion reasonably drawn from multiple established facts, with the reasoning made explicit
Unverified matter	A claim for which the available material is presently insufficient to establish the relevant fact
Contradiction or discrepancy	Two or more records, statements or actions that appear inconsistent and require reconciliation
These classifications are not a hierarchy in which official findings are automatically superior to all other evidence. They are tools for making the report transparent.
An official letter proves that the letter was issued and that its author made the statements recorded in it. It does not automatically prove every underlying allegation. Conversely, a decision not to investigate does not prove that the underlying allegations were false.
3. Why the Federal Court letter must be examined prominently
The 27 March 2023 correspondence from Scott Tredwell, General Counsel of the Federal Court of Australia, is a particularly important point in the chronology.
The letter was issued through the Federal Court’s Public Interest Disclosure process. It is therefore not merely a private opinion or an informal response. It is an official institutional communication concerning a disclosure made under a Commonwealth statutory framework.
The archive transcription identifies three categories of alleged disclosable conduct:
	•	Perverting the course of justice.
	•	Maladministration.
	•	Danger to health or safety.
The letter records that the authorised officer found it difficult to determine whether the belief that the information tended to show such conduct was based on reasonable grounds. For the purpose of the initial assessment, however, he was prepared to assume that the conduct described was disclosable.
The letter then records a decision not to allocate the disclosure to an agency. It states that the Federal Court and the Federal Circuit and Family Court would take no further action under the PID Act on the material.
Three separate matters must therefore be kept visible:
First — the seriousness of the categories recorded. These were not ordinary expressions of dissatisfaction. They were categories expressly recognised by the statutory public-interest disclosure framework.
Second — the procedural decision. The authorised officer did not allocate the disclosure for handling by an agency. That decision ended the Federal Court’s PID Act action on the material, according to the letter.
Third — the unresolved substance. The letter did not determine whether the alleged conduct occurred. It did not establish that the allegations were false. It did not provide the requested investigation or protection.
The distinction between perverting the course of justice and conspiracy must also be maintained. They are not interchangeable legal terms. The fact that the letter records the former does not mean it expressly admits the latter. But neither does the absence of the word conspiracy in that letter dispose of the broader conspiracy allegation. That question must be examined against the full body of communications, decisions, relationships, timing and other evidence.
The Federal Court’s own published PID policy explains the statutory allocation process and the responsibilities of authorised officers. The legislation also provides for allocation or, in specified circumstances, a decision not to allocate. These provisions make the recorded decision examinable; they do not make the underlying allegations disappear. fedcourt.gov.au +1
Preliminary evidentiary conclusion: The 27 March 2023 letter is direct evidence that serious categories of alleged wrongdoing were put before an authorised officer of the Federal Court, that the officer assumed for initial assessment that the conduct could be disclosable, and that the disclosure was nevertheless not allocated. It is not a judicial determination of the truth or falsity of the underlying allegations. It is a significant institutional event requiring examination in the full chronology.
4. The documentary corpus and public archive
The report will use the public archive as an evidentiary collection, not as an unquestionable authority. Its contents must be traceable to the underlying documents wherever possible.
The principal public repositories are:
	•	Barran Dodger — primary archive on GitHub⁠
	•	Public-facing archive website⁠
	•	Official Government Documents Register⁠
	•	Rebuilt archive⁠
	•	Federal Court letter analysis⁠
The archive contains material relating to public-interest disclosures, government correspondence, administrative decisions, oversight complaints, tribunal proceedings, financial administration, disability services, housing and support arrangements, and requests for external scrutiny.
The report will not treat an archive filename, catalogue entry, download count or author’s description as a substitute for the original document. Where an original document is available, it is the primary source. Where only an extract or archive description is available, that limitation must be stated.
The archive’s scale and preservation history are relevant to the history of the evidence, but the number of files or downloads does not independently prove the allegations contained in them.

The following is the initial chronology to be expanded through examination of the original records. It is not a finding that every event was unlawful. It identifies the documentary events and institutional responses that require analysis.

6. The central questions of institutional accountability
The report will examine the following questions as evidentiary issues, not as rhetorical exercises designed to excuse the institutions involved.
6.1 Receipt and recognition
	•	What disclosures and complaints were actually received?
	•	Which officers or agencies acknowledged them?
	•	What conduct did the records say was alleged?
	•	Did the receiving institution identify the seriousness of the allegations?
	•	Did it record the evidence supplied or merely summarise the complainant’s position?
6.2 Investigation and referral
	•	What investigative steps were taken?
	•	What material was examined?
	•	Were relevant witnesses, documents or agencies contacted?
	•	Were matters referred to another body?
	•	If no referral occurred, what reason was recorded?
	•	Was the complainant told of an alternative pathway that was genuinely available?
6.3 Institutional knowledge
	•	Which institutions knew about the allegations?
	•	When did they know?
	•	Did later decisions occur after that knowledge was recorded?
	•	Did the same information circulate between agencies?
	•	Are there records showing communication, coordination or common decision-making?
6.4 Protection and consequences
	•	What protection was requested?
	•	What protection was available under the relevant framework?
	•	Was protection provided, refused, restricted or left unresolved?
	•	What happened to the complainant after the requests?
	•	Can the sequence of decisions and consequences be established through contemporaneous records?
6.5 Possible corruption, collusion and conspiracy
These matters will not be excluded merely because they are serious allegations. Nor will they be treated as established merely because a sequence of adverse events occurred.
The examination must look for evidence such as:
	•	Communications between people or institutions concerning the complainant.
	•	Evidence of common purpose or coordinated action.
	•	Decisions inconsistent with recorded policy or statutory duties.
	•	Misrepresentation of material facts.
	•	Selective treatment of evidence.
	•	Unexplained departures from ordinary procedure.
	•	Concealment, destruction, alteration or withholding of records.
	•	Retaliatory conduct following protected or public-interest disclosures.
	•	Financial, personal or institutional interests connected to the decisions.
	•	Repeated actions whose timing and interrelationship may support an inference of coordination.
The report will state what each item establishes, what it does not establish, and what follows when the items are examined together.
7. Terminology and analytical framework
The report will retain the concepts central to the original commission rather than replacing them with softer or less informative language.
The principal concepts include:
	•	Administrative annihilation.
	•	Civil death.
	•	Civil erasure.
	•	Civil and administrative exclusion.
	•	Institutional complicity.
	•	Conspiracy.
	•	Police corruption.
	•	Social erasure.
	•	Social death.
	•	Societal mobbing.
	•	Corruption.
	•	Institutional retaliation.
	•	Administrative obstruction.
	•	Procedural exclusion.
	•	Denial of effective remedy.
	•	Institutional abandonment.
	•	Documentary suppression or non-disclosure.
	•	Financial disempowerment.
	•	Loss of practical independence.
	•	Cumulative institutional harm.
These terms must be defined carefully. Some are legal concepts, some are social-scientific concepts, and some are analytical descriptions. The report will not pretend that every descriptive concept is a criminal offence. It will examine whether the documented conduct fits the relevant definition and identify the evidence supporting that assessment.
The original commission’s additional catalogues of 85 techniques, 50 phrases and 26 further additions are to be preserved and incorporated into the expanded analytical framework. They should not be silently omitted or reduced to a handful of generic examples. Each item must be defined, connected to its relevant evidence where available, and distinguished from a proven finding.
8. International and historical comparison
The historical comparison will examine the treatment of whistleblowers, public-interest disclosers, dissenters and people alleging institutional wrongdoing. It will consider the difference between:
	•	A person making a disclosure and a person whose disclosure is formally recognised under a statutory scheme.
	•	A complaint being received and a complaint being investigated.
	•	An allegation being recorded and an allegation being substantiated.
	•	An institution refusing to act and an institution establishing that the allegation was false.
	•	A person being excluded from an institutional process and a person receiving an effective remedy.
The comparison will draw on established public-interest disclosure frameworks, human-rights principles, administrative accountability and historical examples. It will not equate Barran Dodger’s circumstances with another person’s case without examining the relevant facts.
9. Preliminary findings from Part I
The initial documentary examination supports the following limited but important conclusions:
	•	The Federal Court’s 27 March 2023 letter is an official record of a public-interest disclosure assessment.
	•	That letter records allegations within three serious statutory categories: perverting the course of justice, maladministration and danger to health or safety.
	•	The authorised officer was prepared to assume for the initial assessment that the conduct described could be disclosable.
	•	The authorised officer then declined to allocate the disclosure and stated that no further action would be taken under the PID Act by the Federal Court or FCFCOA on that material.
	•	The letter does not determine whether the underlying allegations were true or false.
	•	It does not itself establish a conspiracy, but it cannot be used to dismiss the wider conspiracy allegation without examining the other evidence.
	•	The letter’s reasoning concerning public-official status and the employment information it records requires close examination against the underlying correspondence and subsequent records.
	•	The previous report’s broad conclusion that conspiracy was not established by the material examined was premature if this significant document and the wider evidentiary chain had not been adequately examined.
The report must therefore proceed from the documentary record, not from institutional deference.
End of Part I. The next part is the detailed institutional chronology, beginning with the 2021 records and proceeding through the Federal Court assessment and subsequent oversight responses. The source links will be placed beside the relevant events and claims, with the original records distinguished from archive descriptions and later interpretations.


THE WHISTLEBLOWER, THE WITNESS AND THE STATE

PART II — THE CHRONOLOGY: DISCLOSURE, COMPLAINT, INSTITUTIONAL RESPONSE AND CONSEQUENCE

10. Method for examining the chronology

The chronology must not be reduced to a list of agencies that received correspondence. The central issue is what each institution knew, what it did with that knowledge, what it recorded, what it declined to do, and what consequences followed.

Each event will therefore be examined under six headings:

	•	Date and source — the original document, its author, recipient and date.
	•	Information conveyed — what the complainant actually reported or disclosed.
	•	Institutional knowledge — what the receiving body acknowledged or recorded.
	•	Institutional action — what it investigated, referred, decided, refused or left unresolved.
	•	Evidentiary significance — what the record establishes and what may reasonably be inferred.
	•	Outstanding verification — any missing original, attachment, response or contextual record needed to complete the assessment.

A refusal, jurisdictional limitation or non-allocation will be recorded as an institutional action. It will not be transformed into proof that the underlying complaint lacked substance.

The 2021 material is important because it precedes the later Federal Court assessment. The chronology should not begin in March 2023 as though the disclosure appeared without a history.

Verification limitation: The PDF itself has not yet been fully examined in this report. Its title and catalogue entry establish the existence of the archived file, not the exact allegations, evidence enclosed, or the Ombudsman’s response.

	•	IR8415987 report — archived PDF⁠
	•	Archive narrative referencing the hospital record⁠

The original clinical and incident records must be examined directly before making a definitive medical or causal finding.

	•	What was the recorded sequence of events?

	•	What notifications, investigations or incident reviews followed?

The report will not minimise the seriousness of the medical event. Equally, it will not attribute deliberate causation to a particular person without evidence establishing that connection.

12. 2022 — Freedom of information, complaint handling and the distinction between access and accountability

12.1 Victorian Ombudsman — 14 June 2022

The Victorian Ombudsman document is one of the records examined in the archive’s October 2026 evidentiary paper.

	•	Victorian Ombudsman FOI decision — 14 June 2022⁠
	•	Evidentiary examination — section 7.1⁠

The extracted decision relies on section 29A of the Ombudsman Act 1973 (Vic). The provision excludes specified complaint, investigation and related material from the operation of the Victorian FOI Act.

The same document contains a request listing Victorian bodies and describing the author’s complaints and experiences. The archive’s examination correctly distinguishes the requester’s characterisations from the Ombudsman’s own statements.

What the record establishes:

	•	An official Victorian Ombudsman document exists in the archive.
	•	Its extracted decision text invokes section 29A.
	•	The request within the document identifies records sought about Richard McLean and names a number of Victorian bodies.
	•	The statutory exclusion was relied upon in responding to the access request.

What it does not establish: The FOI response does not, by itself, establish that the underlying complaints were investigated, that the alleged events occurred, or that the named bodies committed wrongdoing.

Why it matters: Access to complaint material and investigation of the underlying complaint are different questions. An FOI exclusion may explain why material was not released. It does not answer whether the complaint was properly handled.

That distinction must remain visible throughout the report.

12.2 The Prime Minister and Cabinet FOI pathway

The archive’s research paper identifies a Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet decision concerning FOI-2022-045. The described decision relied on section 24A(1)(b) of the Freedom of Information Act 1982 (Cth), on the basis that documents could not be found or did not exist following searches.

	•	PM&C and FOI material — archive register⁠
	•	PhD research paper — section 8.2⁠

The report must distinguish three propositions:

	•	An agency says it cannot locate or does not hold documents.
	•	The documents do not exist.
	•	The underlying event or conduct never occurred.

Those propositions are not equivalent.

An unsuccessful search may establish the agency’s recorded search outcome. It does not automatically establish the historical non-existence of the information sought, particularly where another agency may hold relevant records.

Evidentiary issue: The search scope, repositories searched, search terms, record-retention practices and any subsequent document releases must be examined before drawing conclusions about the completeness of the search.

12.3 VOCAT and the Ombudsman — 5 October 2022

The archive identifies a document titled VOCAT Ombudsman Ben Calder Complaint Rejection — Fatal Injury.

- VOCAT/Ombudsman document — 5 October 2022⁠

The document title indicates a complaint response associated with a fatal-injury matter. The original PDF must be read before its exact reasoning, legal basis and institutional responsibility can be described.

Documented catalogue fact: The file exists under that title in the public repository.

Author allegation: The author regards the response as part of a wider failure to investigate or address the injury-related concerns.

Outstanding examination: The exact complaint, the decision-maker, the scope of the decision, any jurisdictional or procedural ground relied upon, and any alternative remedy identified.

A complaint rejection is not a factual determination that the event complained of did not occur. Nor does the fact that a complaint was rejected establish that the rejection was improper. The actual reasons and the material considered must be examined.

	•	Danger to health or safety.

Unresolved evidentiary issue: The relationship between the employment acknowledgment and the subsequent public-official conclusion.

Not established by this letter: A judicial finding of conspiracy, a finding that the alleged conduct occurred, or a grant of protected-disclosure status.

That is the precise finding. It is substantial enough without being exaggerated.

14. 2024 — Guardianship, financial management and the loss of practical independence

14.1 NSW Trustee and Guardian — section 122 certificate, 16 October 2024

- NSW Trustee and Guardian section 122 document⁠

The archive’s research paper identifies this as a notice under section 122(2) of the NSW Trustee and Guardian Act 2009 (NSW), concerning management status.

The existence of a statutory certificate is important because it places financial or estate management within a formal legal framework. The exact operative content must be read from the certificate itself.

The report must distinguish:

	•	The existence of a management arrangement.
	•	The legal authority and scope of that arrangement.
	•	The specific powers exercised.
	•	The person’s wishes and participation.
	•	The decisions made about income, expenditure and property.
	•	The mechanisms for review, variation or termination.
	•	The practical effect on the person’s independence.

A certificate recording management status does not, by itself, establish that every later financial decision was lawful, reasonable or consistent with the person’s interests.

Equally, the existence of financial management does not prove corruption. The question is whether the powers were properly exercised and whether the decisions and their consequences can be justified by the records.

14.2 NSW Police complaint response — 24 August 2024

The archive’s research synthesis identifies a NSW Police complaint response dated 24 August 2024.

This document is listed in the archive’s institutional chronology, but its full contents have not been reproduced in the present section.

The report must examine the exact complaint, the allegations made, the response, the police officers or units involved, any investigation undertaken and the stated outcome.

The distinction between a police complaint response and a finding of misconduct is essential. A response may establish what police say they did. It does not automatically establish that the investigation was complete or that the complaint’s underlying allegations were disproved.

What remains to be established: Whether those processes were coordinated, whether particular decisions were improperly influenced, whether any officer acted dishonestly, and whether the combined pattern meets a legal definition of conspiracy or corruption.

Operative wording extracted
