They can affect the ability to obtain:
	•	Food.
	•	Medication.
	•	Transport.
	•	Accommodation.
	•	Communication services.
	•	Legal assistance.
	•	Personal necessities.
	•	Support for an assistance animal.
Where a person is subject to financial administration, the examination should identify the legal authority, the person’s access to funds, the decision-making arrangements and the process for obtaining money for essential needs.
The relevant NSW Trustee records include:
	•	Section 122 document, 16 October 2024⁠.
	•	Vehicle disposal decision, 14 November 2025⁠.
The full financial assessment requires bank statements, transaction histories, payment records, asset valuations, expenditure decisions, requests for funds and responses.
A decision to restrict access to money may be lawful in a particular arrangement. That does not remove the need to examine whether essential needs were met and whether the person had an accessible process for requesting funds and challenging decisions.
Analytical finding: Financial administration must be evaluated not only by whether money was technically managed, but also by whether the arrangement preserved the person’s practical ability to live with dignity and meet essential needs.
182. CRPD Article 28: adequate living conditions and social protection
Article 28 recognises the right of persons with disabilities to an adequate standard of living and social protection without discrimination on the basis of disability.
It includes access to adequate food, clothing and housing, and access to social protection programmes and poverty-reduction measures.
Official text: CRPD, Article 28⁠.
This provision connects the issues examined in the preceding sections.
A person may have an approved disability support plan but still experience inadequate housing. A person may have a source of income but lack practical access to the funds. A person may be formally connected to a service provider but receive insufficient assistance to meet daily needs.
These are not necessarily separate problems.
They can interact and compound one another.
For example:
	•	Restricted access to funds can make transport difficult.
	•	Transport difficulties can interfere with access to medical appointments and support services.
	•	Reduced access to support can make housing arrangements less sustainable.
	•	Housing instability can increase dependence on emergency services.
	•	Financial and housing insecurity can make it more difficult to pursue legal or administrative remedies.
This is a cumulative-harm model. It does not automatically prove that an institution intended to cause the outcome. It provides a framework for examining the practical consequences of decisions and omissions.
The relevant inquiry is whether the State’s disability, housing, financial and social-protection systems operated together to provide an adequate standard of living.
183. CRPD Article 21: freedom of expression and access to information
Article 21 recognises the right of persons with disabilities to freedom of expression and opinion, including the freedom to seek, receive and impart information and ideas on an equal basis with others.
Official text: CRPD, Article 21⁠.
This provision is relevant to the preservation and publication of documentary evidence.
A person seeking to communicate allegations of institutional misconduct should be able to access appropriate communication channels and receive information in accessible forms.
The report must nevertheless distinguish the right to communicate from a claim that every allegation published is necessarily accurate.
The relevant questions include:
	•	Was the person able to obtain records relevant to their own affairs?
	•	Were reasons for decisions communicated?
	•	Were documents supplied in an accessible form?
	•	Were requests for information processed appropriately?
	•	Were restrictions on communication lawful and proportionate?
	•	Did the person have a meaningful opportunity to correct errors?
	•	Could the person communicate concerns without unreasonable barriers?
Freedom of expression is not unlimited. Privacy, confidentiality, defamation law and other legitimate restrictions may apply.
But those limits should not be used as a blanket reason to avoid examining public-interest allegations.
184. The right to privacy, dignity and protection of personal information
Article 17 of the ICCPR protects individuals against arbitrary or unlawful interference with privacy, family, home or correspondence and against unlawful attacks on honour and reputation.
Official text: ICCPR, Article 17⁠.
The CRPD also requires respect for privacy under Article 22.
CRPD, Article 22⁠.
This matters in a documentary archive containing medical, disability, financial, guardianship and personal information.
Preserving evidence does not require publishing every sensitive record without restriction.
A responsible archive should distinguish:
	•	Material necessary to establish an institutional decision.
	•	Personal information incidental to that decision.
	•	Medical details relevant to a specific allegation.
	•	Information about third parties.
	•	Information subject to legal restrictions.
	•	Information that can be redacted without destroying evidentiary meaning.
The objective should be to preserve the original record securely while publishing an appropriately limited version where necessary.
This approach protects both evidentiary integrity and personal dignity.
185. Protection against torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 7 of the ICCPR prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
The Convention against Torture establishes more detailed obligations concerning prevention, investigation and accountability for torture.
Official instruments:
	•	ICCPR, Article 7⁠.
	•	Convention against Torture⁠.
These are serious legal categories.
Not every episode of distress, neglect, poor administration, disability discrimination or institutional conflict reaches the threshold of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.
The legal assessment must consider the nature and severity of the conduct, the circumstances, the relevant actors, the applicable legal elements and any required connection to public authority.
For this report, allegations involving serious injury, threats, neglect, psychological harm or institutional mistreatment should be examined against contemporaneous records.
The inquiry should establish:
	•	What conduct is alleged?
	•	Who is said to have engaged in it?
	•	When and where did it occur?
	•	What contemporaneous evidence exists?
	•	What injury or suffering was documented?
	•	What did responsible institutions know?
	•	What action was taken?
	•	Was there an independent investigation?
	•	What remedy or recovery support was provided?
The report should not use the language of torture as a rhetorical substitute for the legal analysis.
Equally, the seriousness of an allegation should not be minimised merely because the relevant institution has not made a formal finding.
186. The international framework for protection of whistleblowers
The United Nations Convention against Corruption contains provisions relevant to reporting corruption and protecting people who report in good faith.
Article 33 encourages States Parties to consider incorporating appropriate measures to protect reporting persons from unjustified treatment.
Article 35 addresses compensation for damage resulting from acts of corruption.
Official text: United Nations Convention against Corruption⁠.
The Council of Europe has also adopted Recommendation CM/Rec(2014)7 concerning the protection of whistleblowers.
Source: Council of Europe — Recommendation CM/Rec(2014)7⁠.
These international standards provide comparative guidance. They do not automatically determine the legal outcome of an Australian complaint.
The Australian Public Interest Disclosure Act 2013 provides a domestic framework for qualifying public interest disclosures and protections against reprisals.
Public Interest Disclosure Act 2013⁠.
The statutory inquiry must distinguish:
	•	Whether a disclosure met the statutory definition.
	•	Whether it was made to an authorised recipient.
	•	Whether the person making it qualified for protection.
	•	Whether detriment occurred.
	•	Whether the detriment was connected to the disclosure.
	•	Whether the statutory protection and remedy provisions applied.
A disclosure may be important in the public interest without necessarily satisfying every technical requirement of a particular statutory protection scheme.
That distinction must be examined rather than assumed.
187. The problem of fragmented accountability
One of the most important issues raised by the documentary chronology is the possibility that responsibility became fragmented across institutions.
Different agencies may have dealt with different parts of the reported events:
	•	A police agency may have considered a criminal complaint.
	•	An integrity body may have considered whether the conduct fell within its jurisdiction.
	•	An ombudsman may have considered administrative conduct.
	•	A department may have considered a public interest disclosure.
	•	A tribunal may have considered guardianship or administrative review.
	•	A disability agency may have considered support eligibility.
	•	A financial administrator may have made decisions about money and property.
Each institution may have had a legitimate jurisdictional boundary.
But the existence of multiple boundaries creates a further question:
Who was responsible for ensuring that the overall problem received an effective examination?
A fragmented system can produce a situation in which every institution deals with a limited component while no institution examines the complete sequence.
This possibility should be tested against actual referral records and communications.
The following records are particularly important:
	•	Referral letters between institutions.
	•	Internal correspondence about jurisdiction.
	•	Records identifying which agency was responsible for each allegation.
	•	Decisions to transfer, close or decline matters.
	•	Records of whether an alternative agency was contacted.
	•	Any explanation provided to the complainant about the next available process.
The distinction between legitimate jurisdictional separation and a failure of overall accountability is central.
A pattern of separate decisions is not proof of coordination. It may, however, expose a systemic accountability gap requiring examination.
188. The relationship between administrative justice and human dignity
Human dignity is not simply a ceremonial principle.
It has practical implications for how public authorities exercise power.
An administrative decision may affect a person’s:
	•	Housing.
	•	Financial independence.
	•	Health.
	•	Family and personal relationships.
	•	Access to legal assistance.
	•	Ability to communicate.
	•	Participation in the community.
	•	Sense of security and personal autonomy.
The greater the practical effect of a decision, the more important it becomes to examine the decision’s authority, reasoning, procedural fairness and consequences.
The report therefore adopts a cumulative rather than isolated approach.
It is insufficient to consider each administrative decision without examining the relationship between them.
For example, a decision concerning finances may affect access to transport. Transport may affect the ability to attend appointments. Appointment attendance may affect access to support. Support may affect housing stability.
The combined consequences can be substantially more serious than the apparent effect of any single decision.
This does not remove the need to establish causation. It makes the causal investigation more complete.
189. Applying the international framework to the documentary record
The following matrix identifies the principal international-rights questions and the records required to examine them.
Human-rights subject	Relevant instrument	Evidence required
Effective remedy	ICCPR Article 2(3)	Complaints, decisions, reasons, referrals and review rights
Legal capacity	CRPD Article 12	Orders, assessments, reasons and support arrangements
Access to justice	CRPD Article 13	Applications, legal correspondence and procedural accommodations
Protection from abuse	CRPD Article 16	Incident records, risk assessments and investigations
Independent living	CRPD Article 19	Housing assessments, support approvals and delivery records
Privacy	ICCPR Article 17; CRPD Article 22	Disclosure decisions, privacy notices and access records
Adequate living conditions	ICESCR Article 11; CRPD Article 28	Income, housing, food, expenditure and support records
Freedom of expression	CRPD Article 21	Communication restrictions, access to information and correspondence
Whistleblower protection	UNCAC Article 33; Australian PID Act	Original disclosure, statutory assessment and detriment evidence
The matrix is an investigative framework, not a declaration that every listed right has been violated.
The evidence must be matched to the relevant legal test.
190. The cumulative-harm assessment
The report proposes a structured assessment of cumulative harm.
Stage 1 — Identify the events
List each relevant decision, omission, incident, restriction or institutional response.
Stage 2 — Establish the documentary foundation
Identify the original record, its provenance, the author, date, operative content and limitations.
Stage 3 — Establish institutional knowledge
Determine which decision-makers knew about the person’s circumstances, risks, support needs and previous complaints.
Stage 4 — Establish consequences
Identify the effect on housing, finances, health, safety, independence, relationships and access to remedies.
Stage 5 — Examine causation
Determine whether the relevant decision or omission caused, contributed to or aggravated the consequence.
Stage 6 — Examine alternatives
Consider other explanations, intervening events, available resources and the person’s own choices.
Stage 7 — Examine intent and coordination
Where evidence warrants it, investigate improper purpose, retaliation, improper influence or coordinated conduct.
Stage 8 — Identify remedies
Consider restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, restoration of access, corrective decisions, independent review and guarantees of non-repetition.
This approach avoids two opposite errors:
	•	Treating every adverse event as proof of a coordinated campaign.
	•	Treating every adverse event as unrelated simply because it was handled by a different institution.
191. Findings of Part XIV
The following findings emerge from the international framework and the documentary material identified in the preceding parts.
Finding 1 — Effective remedy is a central issue.
The sequence of complaint processes and institutional closures requires examination of whether an accessible and effective overall remedy was available.
Finding 2 — Legal capacity and autonomy require particular scrutiny.
Financial administration and guardianship decisions should be examined for authority, proportionality, safeguards and respect for the person’s will and preferences.
Finding 3 — Access to justice must be practical.
The existence of formal complaint and review processes does not, by itself, establish that a person with disability-related support needs could realistically use them.
Finding 4 — Disability support must be assessed by actual delivery.
An approved plan budget is not equivalent to the provision of accommodation, support workers or practical independence.
Finding 5 — Housing and financial security are interconnected.
A proper assessment must consider whether decisions and service arrangements, taken together, enabled an adequate standard of living.
Finding 6 — Protection from abuse requires evidence-led investigation.
Serious incident and mistreatment allegations should be tested against original records, risk assessments, investigation files and contemporaneous evidence.
Finding 7 — Fragmented institutional responsibility can create accountability gaps.
Whether that occurred in this matter requires examination of interagency referrals, communications and the complete complaint history.
Finding 8 — International standards do not replace domestic legal tests.
The CRPD, ICCPR, ICESCR and UNCAC provide relevant standards, but any conclusion about domestic legal liability must identify the applicable Australian law.
Finding 9 — Cumulative consequences deserve examination.
Separate decisions may have combined to produce a serious practical effect. That possibility must be investigated without assuming a common purpose.
Finding 10 — The remedy must address the actual harm.
Where wrongdoing is established, a response limited to acknowledging receipt of a complaint may be inadequate. The appropriate remedy depends on the violation, the consequences and the available legal framework.
192. Conclusion: rights must operate in reality
The international human-rights framework establishes that people with disabilities are rights-holders, not merely recipients of institutional care.
It recognises legal capacity, access to justice, independent living, protection from abuse, privacy, freedom of expression and adequate living conditions.
These principles provide a serious framework for examining the documentary record.
The central question is whether the institutions involved provided practical protection and effective remedies, not merely whether individual files were opened, processed or closed.
The report does not need to presume that every allegation is established in order to recognise that the questions are substantial.
Nor should an absence of formal findings be mistaken for an absence of evidence requiring examination.
The documentary record must be assessed on its contents, provenance, context and corroboration.
Where a record establishes an institutional decision, that decision can be examined. Where records conflict, the conflict can be investigated. Where a process ended without resolving the substantive allegation, that limitation should be accurately recorded.
Human rights are not meaningful if they exist only on paper.
Time is the witness. Truth is the judge.
END OF PART XIV
Next: PART XV — THE INVESTIGATION OF INSTITUTIONAL COORDINATION: INTERAGENCY COMMUNICATIONS, COMMON PURPOSE, DECISION-MAKER KNOWLEDGE, RETALIATION, CONSPIRACY AND THE EVIDENCE REQUIRED TO DISTINGUISH SYSTEMIC FAILURE FROM DELIBERATE MISCONDUCT.

THE WHISTLEBLOWER, THE WITNESS AND THE STATE
PART XV — THE INVESTIGATION OF INSTITUTIONAL COORDINATION
193. The central investigative question
This part examines one of the most serious issues raised by the documentary chronology: whether the institutional decisions affecting Barran Dodger were independent administrative actions, manifestations of systemic failure, or actions connected through communication, influence, common purpose or improper coordination.
The question must be investigated rather than predetermined.
A sequence of decisions made by different institutions does not, by itself, prove conspiracy. Equally, the fact that decisions were formally issued by different institutions does not establish that they were independent of one another.
Institutions can communicate. Officials can exchange information. Decisions can be influenced by earlier decisions. Complaints can be referred, redirected or discussed. A common narrative can develop across agencies, whether through legitimate information-sharing or through improper influence.
The existence, nature and purpose of any such connections are matters for documentary examination.
The central distinction is:
	•	Institutional sequence: several institutions take actions over time.
	•	Institutional interdependence: one institution’s action affects another institution’s decision.
	•	Institutional coordination: institutions or individuals communicate or arrange their actions in relation to a matter.
	•	Improper coordination: coordination is undertaken for an improper purpose or through an improper process.
	•	Criminal conspiracy: an agreement satisfying the elements of an applicable criminal offence.
These are different propositions. Evidence sufficient to establish one does not automatically establish the next.
194. The Federal Court PID letter: the starting point for examining the disclosure history
The Federal Court correspondence dated 27 March 2023 is important because it records that serious allegations had been brought to the attention of an authorised officer considering a public interest disclosure matter.
The letter identifies alleged categories including:
	•	Perverting the course of justice.
	•	Maladministration.
	•	Conduct endangering health or safety.
It records that the officer considered it difficult to determine whether there were reasonable grounds but was prepared, for the initial assessment, to assume that the described conduct could be disclosable.
The letter subsequently declines allocation and states that no further action under the PID Act would be taken by the Federal Court or Federal Circuit and Family Court on the material.
It also records information concerning DSS employment status before expressing a conclusion that the officer was not satisfied the disclosure had been made by a public official.
These passages create specific questions about the statutory assessment and the information relied upon.
Primary document:
27 March 2023 — Federal Court PID assessment⁠
Related analysis:
Examination of the Federal Court letter⁠
The letter is an official administrative record. It is not a judicial judgment establishing that the alleged conduct occurred. It does not itself establish a criminal conspiracy.
But it is evidence that the allegations were placed before an institutional decision-maker and that a particular assessment and non-allocation decision followed.
That makes the underlying disclosure, attachments, assessment notes and referral history important investigative material.
195. The November 2021 Commonwealth Ombudsman PID assessment: correcting institutional attribution
The document dated 18 November 2021 has an important provenance issue.
Its filename refers to IBAC, but the document itself identifies the Commonwealth Ombudsman Public Interest Disclosure Team as the issuing body.
It refers to PID-2021-400008-R and records an assessment of whether the information met the Commonwealth PID Act requirements.
The document therefore must not be attributed to IBAC merely because of its filename.
Primary document:
18 November 2021 — Commonwealth Ombudsman PID-2021-400008-R⁠
Related examination:
Commonwealth Ombudsman PID assessment⁠
The letter records that the Ombudsman reviewed an authorised officer’s decision and agreed that the information did not satisfy the relevant Commonwealth PID requirements. The reasons included the absence of information demonstrating disclosable conduct by a Commonwealth agency or Commonwealth public official.
This is significant because it identifies a jurisdictional and statutory assessment, not necessarily an investigation into every factual allegation.
The proper questions are:
	•	What was the original disclosure?
	•	Which conduct and entities did it identify?
	•	Which statutory criteria were applied?
	•	What information was considered?
	•	Was the distinction between Commonwealth and State responsibilities correctly applied?
	•	Were any matters referred to another body?
	•	Were the reasons and available review rights communicated?
	•	Did later institutions rely on this assessment, and if so, how?
The correction of the filename is not a minor issue. It demonstrates why source attribution must be verified against the actual document rather than inferred from archive labels.
196. A decision-making chain: how institutional influence can be tested
An investigation of coordination should reconstruct the complete decision-making chain.
For each relevant decision, identify:
	•	The person who made it.
	•	The person who recommended it.
	•	The person who supplied information.
	•	The records available to the decision-maker.
	•	The information that was excluded.
	•	The institution’s stated reason.
	•	Any communication with another institution.
	•	The timing of the decision relative to other events.
	•	Any later change in the decision or its explanation.
This is necessary because the official signatory is not necessarily the only person who influenced the decision.
A decision may have been prepared by one officer, reviewed by another, approved by a manager and informed by correspondence from an external institution.
That process is not inherently improper. It is a normal feature of administration.
But where a serious allegation concerns improper influence, the actual chain must be examined rather than stopping at the signature on the final letter.
The person who signed the decision, the person who made the recommendation and the person who supplied decisive information may be different individuals.
The records should identify each role.
197. The evidence of interagency communication
The most direct way to investigate institutional coordination is to obtain the communications connecting the relevant institutions.
The investigation should seek:
	•	Emails between the relevant agencies.
	•	Internal memoranda.
	•	Referral letters.
	•	Case-management notes.
	•	Meeting records.
	•	Telephone attendance notes.
	•	Briefings prepared for senior officials.
	•	Attachments exchanged between agencies.
	•	Requests for advice.
	•	Records of decisions made following external contact.
	•	Records identifying who authorised a referral or information exchange.
	•	Records of any restrictions placed on further communication.
The investigation should also examine communications held by the recipient agency, not just the institution that allegedly sent them.
A record may be absent from one agency’s disclosure but preserved in another agency’s file.
Where possible, searches should include:
	•	The complainant’s full name and known variations.
	•	Relevant complaint and case references.
	•	The names and positions of known decision-makers.
	•	Relevant dates.
	•	Subject headings.
	•	File numbers.
	•	Names of agencies involved.
	•	Known attachment names.
The search should preserve its scope and methodology. A statement that an agency found no records is only meaningful when the locations searched, terms used, date range and record systems are known.
198. Decision-maker knowledge: what did each institution know?
Institutional knowledge is central to examining both administrative responsibility and possible coordination.
An institution cannot be assessed solely by what it says it knew after a complaint. The inquiry should reconstruct what information was available to the relevant decision-makers at the time.
For each significant decision, the investigation should identify:
	•	What allegations had previously been made.
	•	Which supporting documents had been supplied.
	•	Whether the decision-maker had access to earlier complaints.
	•	Whether known risks had been communicated.
	•	Whether the person’s disability-related support needs were recorded.
	•	Whether previous institutional decisions were relied upon.
	•	Whether contrary information was available.
	•	Whether the decision-maker sought clarification.
	•	Whether any relevant information was disregarded or omitted from the reasons.
There is a difference between information held somewhere within an institution and information actually known to the person making a particular decision.
The investigation should not automatically attribute the knowledge of every employee to every other employee. It should establish the relevant organisational arrangements, file access, reporting lines and actual communications.
However, an institution’s internal division of responsibilities should not become an excuse for failing to respond to information that its established procedures required to be escalated.
Forensic question: Was relevant information available to the institution, and did its systems ensure that the people responsible for acting on it received and considered it?
199. Chronology and proximity: why timing matters but does not prove motive
The timing of decisions can be probative.
A decision made shortly after a disclosure, complaint or request for review may justify investigation of a possible connection.
For example, the following sequence may be relevant:
	•	A person makes a protected or potentially protected disclosure.
	•	An institution becomes aware of the disclosure.
	•	The person experiences an adverse decision or detriment.
	•	The decision-maker has access to information about the disclosure.
	•	The institution provides an explanation for the adverse action.
	•	Later records reveal whether the explanation was consistent with the contemporaneous evidence.
This sequence may support an inquiry into reprisal.
It does not automatically establish reprisal. There may be an independent reason for the decision, a pre-existing process or an unrelated event.
The investigation should therefore distinguish:
	•	Temporal proximity.
	•	Decision-maker knowledge.
	•	Adverse treatment.
	•	Causal connection.
	•	Stated reason.
	•	Evidence of improper purpose.
The Commonwealth PID Act 2013 contains a statutory prohibition on taking or threatening reprisal against a person because of a belief or suspicion that the person has made, may have made, or proposes to make a public interest disclosure.
The Act also addresses detriment, including specified forms of harm.
Public Interest Disclosure Act 2013 — current legislation⁠.
The applicable version of the legislation must be checked against the date of each alleged disclosure and reprisal. A current compilation should not simply be applied retrospectively to earlier events.
200. Reprisal: the statutory question must be separated from the broader allegation
A reprisal allegation requires more than showing that an adverse event followed a complaint.
The investigation should establish:
	•	Whether the person made, proposed to make or was believed to have made a disclosure covered by the relevant statutory framework.
	•	Whether the person experienced or was threatened with detriment.
	•	Whether the relevant decision-maker held the required belief or suspicion.
	•	Whether the disclosure-related belief or suspicion was a reason for the conduct.
	•	Whether the statutory provisions applied to the person, recipient, conduct and institution.
	•	Whether any available defence, exception or alternative explanation is relevant.
The relevant statute is the Public Interest Disclosure Act 2013⁠, particularly its provisions concerning reprisal and remedies.
The investigation must also consider whether conduct falls outside the Commonwealth PID Act but may be addressed under another law, employment framework, administrative review process or State legislation.
The fact that a disclosure did not qualify under one statutory scheme does not automatically establish that the underlying conduct was proper. It means that the particular statutory protection may not have been available on that assessment.
This distinction is essential to avoid confusing:
	•	The merits of the underlying allegation.
	•	The legal qualification of the disclosure.
	•	The availability of statutory protection.
	•	The lawfulness of later conduct.
These are related, but separate, questions.
201. Conspiracy: the legal threshold and the evidentiary investigation
The word conspiracy has both an ordinary meaning and a specific legal meaning.
In ordinary language, it may describe a suspicion that people have acted together in secret to achieve an improper objective.
In criminal law, it is a defined offence with specific elements.
Under section 11.5 of the Commonwealth Criminal Code, conspiracy involves an agreement between at least two persons that one or more parties will commit an offence, together with the intention that the offence be committed.
The statutory provisions must be read in full, including the applicable requirements concerning the agreement and the offence contemplated.
Official legislation:
Criminal Code Act 1995 — section 11.5⁠.
A criminal conspiracy allegation therefore requires evidence of more than:
	•	Multiple institutions taking adverse decisions.
	•	Similar wording in separate letters.
	•	Repeated jurisdictional refusals.
	•	A sequence of complaints and administrative restrictions.
	•	The existence of institutional relationships.
	•	An outcome that appears unfair or harmful.
Those circumstances may be relevant evidence, but they do not by themselves establish an agreement to commit a criminal offence.
The investigation should identify:
	•	The alleged participants.
	•	The alleged agreement.
	•	The offence said to be the object of that agreement.
	•	The evidence connecting each participant to the agreement.
	•	The relevant intention.
	•	The timing and circumstances of the agreement.
	•	Any communications, instructions or conduct supporting the inference.
	•	Evidence inconsistent with the allegation.
An agreement need not necessarily be recorded in a single signed document. Circumstantial evidence may be relevant. But the inference must be grounded in the evidence and must satisfy the applicable legal standard.
The absence of an explicit written agreement is not necessarily conclusive. Nor is the presence of suspicious timing or parallel conduct sufficient by itself.
The correct position is neither to declare conspiracy proven without the necessary evidence nor to dismiss the possibility without examining the communications and decision-making records.
202. The difference between coordinated administration and improper coordination
Public institutions regularly coordinate their work.
They may lawfully:
	•	Share information where authorised.
	•	Refer complaints to the appropriate body.
	•	Seek legal advice.
	•	Consult other agencies.
	•	Rely on earlier decisions where legally appropriate.
	•	Coordinate service delivery.
	•	Exchange information to protect safety.
The existence of coordination is therefore not itself evidence of corruption.
The question is whether the coordination was lawful, transparent where required, properly authorised and directed towards a legitimate purpose.
Potential indicators requiring further examination include:
	•	Communications that are inconsistent with the formal reasons subsequently given.
	•	An instruction to reach a predetermined outcome.
	•	Deliberate exclusion of relevant evidence.
	•	An attempt to prevent an authorised investigation.
	•	A decision-maker relying on information they knew to be false.
	•	A referral designed to avoid scrutiny rather than direct the complaint to a competent body.
	•	Retaliatory language in internal correspondence.
	•	A common plan to cause an unlawful detriment.
	•	Alteration or concealment of records.
	•	A decision being changed following an unexplained external intervention.
Each indicator requires context and corroboration.
An apparently unusual communication may have a legitimate explanation. An unexplained change may result from new information. A referral may be entirely proper.
The investigative task is to obtain the underlying records and determine which explanation is supported.
203. Institutional complicity and the failure to act
Institutional complicity is used in this report as an analytical description of situations in which an institution or its personnel may knowingly facilitate, conceal, perpetuate or enable wrongdoing by another actor.
It should not be used as a substitute for identifying the legal responsibility of a particular person or organisation.
Several different situations must be distinguished:
Direct participation: an individual actively engages in the alleged wrongful conduct.
Assistance or facilitation: an individual knowingly provides assistance that contributes to the conduct.
Concealment: an individual knowingly hides relevant information or obstructs accountability.
Failure to act: an institution fails to take action despite having relevant responsibilities and sufficient information.
Systemic failure: organisational arrangements repeatedly fail to prevent, identify or correct a particular type of harm.
Criminal complicity: conduct satisfying the elements of an applicable criminal offence.
A failure to investigate a complaint may be serious maladministration. It is not automatically proof that the institution intended to assist the alleged wrongdoer.
The relevant inquiry must establish the duty, knowledge, available action, omission, consequence and any required mental element.
This approach is important in the examination of the police, oversight bodies, government departments and service providers identified in the archive.
204. The police accountability chain
Police-related allegations require a distinct examination because police agencies have specific powers and responsibilities.
A complaint about police conduct should be reconstructed through the complete administrative and operational record.
The investigation should identify:
	•	The original report.
	•	The date and method of reporting.
	•	The event or incident number.
	•	The officer or unit receiving the report.
	•	The initial classification.
	•	Any risk assessment.
	•	Any decision to investigate, refer or decline.
	•	Evidence collected.
	•	Witnesses contacted.
	•	Supervisory review.
	•	The final outcome.
	•	Reasons provided.
	•	Any review or oversight process.
A response stating that a matter does not fall within a particular agency’s jurisdiction establishes the agency’s stated jurisdictional position. It does not establish that the underlying allegations are false.
The 19 November 2025 LECC letter, reference CASE202512395/13KM, states that the complaint did not concern officers of the NSW Police Force or the NSW Crime Commission and that the LECC could not take action on the information supplied.
Primary document:
LECC response, 19 November 2025⁠.
The letter is evidence of a jurisdictional decision. It is not a substantive finding on the truth of every allegation.
The investigation should determine what complaint was submitted, what conduct and individuals it identified, and whether any other appropriate avenue was communicated.
The NSW Police response dated 24 August 2024 also requires examination in its original form. The archive’s reference to that response is not enough to establish the complete scope of any police investigation.
205. The National Anti-Corruption Commission and the threshold for referral
The National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) is an important Commonwealth integrity body.
Its statutory framework is contained in the National Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2022⁠.
The NACC’s published information explains how corruption information can be reported and how the Commission assesses matters.
National Anti-Corruption Commission — Reporting Corruption⁠.
A complaint to the NACC is not itself a finding of corruption. Acknowledgment, assessment, referral, investigation and final findings are distinct procedural stages.
A properly prepared referral should identify:
	•	The alleged corrupt conduct.
	•	The public official or public body involved, where known.
	•	The relevant public power or function.
	•	The alleged improper purpose or benefit.
	•	The dates and events.
	•	The primary documents.
	•	Any witnesses or corroborating evidence.
	•	Any related investigations or decisions.
	•	The reasons the matter may meet the Commission’s statutory requirements.
The NACC’s jurisdiction and statutory thresholds must be applied to the actual conduct and evidence.
It should not be assumed that every instance of maladministration is corrupt conduct within the NACC’s jurisdiction.
Equally, a matter should not be dismissed merely because the person reporting it cannot identify every participant or obtain internal records that remain held by the institution.
The strongest referral separates the established documentary facts from the allegations and identifies the specific investigative steps needed to resolve the outstanding questions.
206. The evidentiary matrix for institutional coordination
The following matrix provides a practical method for testing the different hypotheses.
Hypothesis	Evidence that would support examination	Evidence that may weaken it
Independent administrative decisions	Separate decision records, distinct evidence and independent reasons	Undisclosed communications or unexplained common instructions
Systemic failure	Repeated procedural errors, fragmented responsibility and recurring omissions	Evidence that the institution identified and corrected the problem
Improper influence	External pressure, unexplained changes or communications inconsistent with formal reasons	Documented lawful advice and independently reasoned decisions
Reprisal	Disclosure knowledge, subsequent detriment and evidence of causal connection	A documented independent reason predating the disclosure
Concealment	Deliberate withholding, destruction or misleading explanations	Complete and consistent disclosure records
Coordinated unlawful conduct	Evidence of agreement, participants, intended offence and relevant intention	Evidence that the actions were independent or lacked the alleged common objective
This matrix is not a verdict. It is a method for directing document requests and witness examination.
The evidence must be assessed as a whole.
207. The records most likely to resolve the coordination question
The following records should be prioritised because they can establish whether the institutional sequence involved communication, influence or common purpose.
Priority 1 — Original disclosure and its complete assessment history
Obtain the original disclosure, every attachment, receipt confirmation, internal assessment, referral and decision concerning the 2021 PID matter.
Priority 2 — Federal Court assessment records
Obtain the complete file underlying the 27 March 2023 letter, including the original material, internal assessment notes, statutory analysis, correspondence and any communications with DSS or other agencies.
Priority 3 — DSS records
Obtain the original DSS employment-related records, the July 2023 PID response, relevant employment or service records, and the correspondence reportedly identified as Exhibit R3.
The purpose is to compare the actual records with the employment-related propositions recorded in the Federal Court assessment.
Priority 4 — Interagency correspondence
Obtain communications between the Commonwealth Ombudsman, Federal Court, DSS, AFP, NSW Police, LECC, NDIA, NDIS Commission, NSW Trustee and Guardian, and other identified bodies where relevant to the same allegations.
This should include both incoming and outgoing communications.
Priority 5 — Police and integrity-body records
Obtain the full NSW Police complaint file, the LECC submission and assessment, and any referral or review documentation.
Priority 6 — Financial and disability-support decisions
Obtain the original NSW Trustee financial records, vehicle disposal valuation and accounting, NDIS requests and assessments, service-delivery records and relevant accommodation correspondence.
These records may establish the practical consequences of decisions and whether the responsible institutions were informed of those consequences.
Priority 7 — Record-management and access history
Where legally available, obtain file-access logs, document-management audit trails, version histories and records identifying who created, amended, viewed or transferred relevant documents.
Such records may help reconstruct the actual sequence of institutional activity.
208. The alternative explanations that must be tested
A serious independent examination must test competing explanations.
At least five hypotheses should be considered.
Hypothesis A — Independent decisions
Each institution made its own decision within its jurisdiction, based on the information available to it.
If this explanation is supported, the report should identify the separate reasons and the evidence on which each decision was based.
Hypothesis B — Systemic fragmentation
The institutions acted within their respective jurisdictions, but the overall system failed to provide a coherent response.
This could occur without any agreement or improper intention.
Hypothesis C — Institutional deference
Later decision-makers relied heavily on earlier institutional conclusions without independently examining the underlying material.
This may create a self-reinforcing administrative narrative, even where no deliberate coordination exists.
Hypothesis D — Improper influence or retaliation
A person or institution influenced decisions for an improper purpose, including possible retaliation for disclosure or complaint activity.
This requires evidence of knowledge, influence, detriment and the applicable causal or mental elements.
Hypothesis E — Deliberate coordinated wrongdoing
Two or more persons entered an agreement to pursue an unlawful objective, or engaged in another form of coordinated misconduct.
This is the most serious hypothesis and requires evidence satisfying the relevant legal elements.
These hypotheses should not be treated as mutually exclusive in every respect. Systemic failure may coexist with individual misconduct. An initially independent process may later be influenced by an external communication.
The purpose of the investigation is to determine which explanation, or combination of explanations, best fits the complete record.
209. What would constitute a meaningful independent investigation?
An independent investigation should not simply ask each institution to reconsider its own previous response.
It should examine the underlying evidence and the connections between decisions.
A credible investigation should have:
	•	An investigator independent of the agencies whose conduct is under examination.
	•	Access to relevant original records.
	•	Authority to obtain interagency communications where legally available.
	•	A clear chronology of disclosures, complaints and decisions.
	•	Identification of decision-makers and relevant advisers.
	•	Examination of the actual reasons for significant decisions.
	•	Comparison of stated reasons with contemporaneous records.
	•	Examination of possible reprisal and improper influence.
	•	Consideration of alternative explanations.
	•	A reasoned report identifying established facts, unresolved matters and any findings within the investigator’s authority.
The investigation should not be confined to whether each agency followed its own internal procedure.
It should examine whether the complete sequence complied with applicable law and whether the combined institutional response produced an unlawful or unjustifiable outcome.
210. Proposed investigative findings and current evidentiary position
On the material identified in the preceding parts, the following conclusions can presently be stated.
Finding 1 — There is a documented sequence of institutional dealings.
The archive identifies complaints, PID assessments, correspondence, jurisdictional decisions and administrative processes extending across multiple years.
Finding 2 — The Federal Court letter records serious allegations.
The 27 March 2023 letter is an official administrative record of the assessment and non-allocation decision. It is not a judicial determination of the alleged conduct.
Finding 3 — The November 2021 PID document was misattributed in its filename.
Its actual institutional source is the Commonwealth Ombudsman, not IBAC. The correction must be maintained throughout the archive and any resulting reports.
Finding 4 — The examined LECC letter records a jurisdictional refusal.
It does not establish that the allegations were false or that another appropriate investigative route was unnecessary.
Finding 5 — The complete interagency communication history remains central.
Without the original communications, referral records, decision-making notes and internal assessments, it is not possible to establish the extent of coordination.
Finding 6 — Possible reprisal warrants examination against the statutory test.
The timing of complaints and subsequent decisions may justify investigation, but timing alone does not establish the causal connection required by the applicable law.
Finding 7 — Systemic administrative failure remains a distinct possibility.
Fragmented responsibility, repeated procedural closure and lack of an overall resolution may indicate systemic deficiencies even if no criminal agreement is established.
Finding 8 — Criminal conspiracy must be tested against section 11.5 of the Criminal Code.
The investigation must establish the alleged agreement, intended offence, participants and relevant intention. The chronology alone does not prove those elements.
Finding 9 — Institutional complicity must be assessed individually.
Each institution’s knowledge, responsibilities, actions and omissions must be established rather than attributed collectively.
Finding 10 — The absence of a completed investigation is not proof that the allegations are false.
It means the relevant propositions remain to be assessed against the available evidence and any applicable findings.
211. Conclusion: coordination must be examined, not assumed away
The documentary chronology presents a legitimate basis for investigating whether the institutional responses were independent, interconnected or influenced by communications and decisions elsewhere.
The correct approach is to obtain the records that reveal how decisions were actually made.
A public authority’s letter is evidence of what that authority communicated. An assessment is evidence of the assessment undertaken. A refusal is evidence of a refusal. A referral is evidence of a referral.
None should be transformed into a finding that it does not contain.
Equally, none should be dismissed merely because it does not conclusively establish the wider allegation.
The possibility of institutional coordination must be investigated through original communications, decision-making records, access histories and evidence of common purpose.
If those records demonstrate independent lawful decisions, that conclusion should be stated.
If they demonstrate systemic fragmentation, that should be stated.
If they demonstrate improper influence, reprisal, concealment or coordinated unlawful conduct, those findings should be identified and supported by the relevant evidence.
No institution should be presumed guilty. No institution should be presumed beyond examination.
The investigative standard must be consistent for every person and every agency.
Preservation First. Examination Second. Conclusion Last.
END OF PART XV
Next: PART XVI — THE FINANCIAL, PROPERTY AND DISABILITY-SUPPORT RECORD: NSW TRUSTEE AND GUARDIAN, VEHICLE DISPOSAL, ACCESS TO FUNDS, NDIS PLAN IMPLEMENTATION, ACCOMMODATION, SIL, SDA AND THE MEASUREMENT OF ACTUAL SUPPORT AGAINST APPROVED SUPPORT.



THE WHISTLEBLOWER, THE WITNESS AND THE STATE
PART XVI — FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION, PROPERTY AND DISABILITY SUPPORT
212. The central question: what was authorised, what was delivered and what was the actual consequence?
This part examines the financial and disability-support records identified in the archive, with particular attention to NSW Trustee and Guardian, financial independence, vehicle disposal, access to money, NDIS funding, accommodation and the distinction between approved support and support actually received.
The central question is not simply whether an institution made a decision.
It is whether the decision was legally authorised, properly reasoned, implemented accurately and consistent with the person’s rights and assessed needs.
Three separate tests must be applied:
	•	Authority: Was the decision-maker legally empowered to make the decision?
	•	Administration: Was the decision made and implemented lawfully, fairly and accurately?
	•	Outcome: Did the decision preserve or impair the person’s practical ability to live safely and independently?
A decision can be legally authorised yet poorly implemented. An approved budget can be substantial yet fail to provide the required services. A financial administration arrangement can be protective in purpose but still require scrutiny of individual restrictions and their consequences.
The report must therefore examine the original records rather than rely solely on summaries, account balances or institutional descriptions.
213. NSW Trustee and Guardian: authority and accountability
The NSW Trustee and Guardian operates under the NSW Trustee and Guardian Act 2009⁠.
The Act provides the statutory framework for the functions and powers of the organisation, including financial management and related responsibilities.
The existence of an appointment or financial management arrangement does not remove the need to examine individual decisions.
The investigation should establish:
	•	The legal instrument authorising the arrangement.
	•	The date the authority commenced.
	•	The precise scope of the powers granted.
	•	Any limitations or conditions.
	•	The person’s rights and available review processes.
	•	The financial records maintained.
	•	The decisions made about income, expenditure and assets.
	•	The procedures for requesting funds.
	•	The arrangements for communicating decisions.
	•	The process for reviewing the continuing need for restrictions.
The question is whether the administration remained within the authority conferred and whether the relevant duties were discharged.
A general statement that the Trustee was acting protectively is not sufficient to resolve a specific dispute about a payment, asset, vehicle or restriction.
Each disputed decision must be examined separately.
214. The section 122 document dated 16 October 2024
The archive identifies a NSW Trustee and Guardian document dated 16 October 2024 and described as a section 122 document.
Primary source:
NSW Trustee and Guardian — 16 October 2024⁠.
The document must be examined in its entirety before conclusions are drawn about its legal effect.
The forensic examination should identify:
	•	The precise statutory provision relied upon.
	•	The identity and authority of the issuing officer.
	•	The person or property to which the document relates.
	•	The action authorised or required.
	•	Any conditions or limitations.
	•	The period for which the authority applied.
	•	The reasons provided.
	•	Any notification or review rights.
	•	Whether the document was implemented.
	•	Whether the person affected received an adequate explanation.
A reference to section 122 in a filename is not, by itself, proof of the precise legal operation of the document. The operative text and the version of the legislation in force at the relevant time must be checked.
The investigation should also compare the document with the underlying order or appointment. An administrative document cannot be interpreted in isolation from the legal instrument that establishes the relevant authority.
215. Financial independence and access to personal funds
Financial independence involves more than having an income recorded on an institutional ledger.
It requires practical access to money for ordinary life.
The archive and prior statements identify concerns involving:
	•	Access to Commonwealth Bank online and mobile banking.
	•	Access to funds through a card or account.
	•	Regular income.
	•	A personal allowance.
	•	Rent and other recurring expenses.
	•	Debt deductions.
	•	Utility payments.
	•	The management and disposal of a vehicle.
These matters require reconciliation against original bank statements and Trustee records.
The reported figures from October 2026 include:
Item	Previously reported amount

The essential question is whether the person had reliable and reasonable access to sufficient funds to meet ordinary needs.
A budget that is fully allocated to institutional payments may leave little practical capacity for unexpected expenses, transport, food or personal necessities.
This does not automatically establish unlawful conduct. It establishes why the actual transaction history and decision-making records must be examined.
216. The vehicle disposal decision dated 14 November 2025
The archive identifies a NSW Trustee vehicle disposal decision dated 14 November 2025.
Primary source:
NSW Trustee — Vehicle Disposal Decision, 14 November 2025⁠.
A vehicle can represent more than a financial asset.
For a person with disability-related support needs, it may also provide:
	•	Transport to medical appointments.
	•	Access to disability services.
	•	Access to food and essential supplies.
	•	Ability to maintain relationships.
	•	Access to employment or other activities.
	•	Independence from public transport.
	•	A means of maintaining accommodation or responding to emergencies.
The decision must therefore be assessed in both financial and practical terms.
The investigation should establish:
	•	Who owned the vehicle?
	•	What legal authority governed its disposal?
	•	What was its market value?
	•	Was an independent valuation obtained?
	•	What sale method was used?
	•	Was the person consulted?
	•	What reasons were given?
	•	What sale price was achieved?
	•	Were costs and deductions recorded?
	•	Where were the proceeds deposited?
	•	Was the final accounting supplied?
	•	What was the effect on transport and independence?
	•	Were alternative arrangements considered?
The financial question is whether the asset was properly managed.
The human-rights and disability-support question is whether the decision and its consequences were assessed in the context of the person’s actual needs.
A vehicle may be sold for legitimate reasons. The sale must nevertheless be transparent, properly authorised and accounted for.
A record showing that a vehicle was disposed of does not, by itself, establish that the disposal was improper. Nor does it establish that the person received an adequate replacement for the transport function the vehicle provided.
217. The difference between managing money and maintaining a person’s life
Financial administration should be assessed against its practical purpose.
The relevant objective is not merely to maintain a balanced ledger. It is to administer the person’s financial affairs consistently with the applicable legal authority and duties while enabling necessary living expenses to be met.
The distinction becomes especially important where a person depends on others to obtain access to their own funds.
The investigation should consider:
	•	Whether requests for money were answered promptly.
	•	Whether the person could obtain funds for food and essentials.
	•	Whether emergency requests were considered.
	•	Whether reasons for restrictions were supplied.
	•	Whether the person could challenge a decision.
	•	Whether the financial arrangement was periodically reviewed.
	•	Whether restrictions were proportionate to the identified risk.
	•	Whether less restrictive arrangements were considered.
A system that records every expenditure but cannot demonstrate that essential needs were met requires further examination.
The question is not whether a financial administrator should exercise appropriate controls. It is whether those controls were lawful, proportionate and responsive to the actual circumstances.
218. NDIS plan approval: the difference between allocation and delivery
The archive identifies an NDIS plan approval dated 20 November 2025 with a total amount of $366,406.69.
Primary source:
NDIS Plan Approval — 20 November 2025⁠.
The previously identified plan categories include:

These figures should be checked against the original plan approval and its detailed schedules before being treated as a definitive financial reconciliation.
The total is evidence of the approved plan amount, not proof that the full amount was spent, that services were available, or that the participant received the required assistance.
The following concepts must remain separate:
	•	Requested: support sought by the participant or representative.
	•	Recommended: support identified by a professional assessment.
	•	Approved: support included in the NDIA plan.
	•	Booked: a service arranged with a provider.
	•	Delivered: support actually provided.
	•	Effective: support that achieved the intended practical outcome.
A plan can be approved without being fully implemented.
A service can be booked but cancelled.
A provider can be engaged without delivering the required hours.
A support can be delivered but still fail to meet the participant’s assessed needs.
The investigation must follow the evidence through each stage.
219. Core supports: funding availability versus practical assistance
The Core Flexible category was previously recorded as $274,255.84.
Core supports can be central to daily living, assistance with personal activities, household tasks, community participation and other supports permitted by the participant’s plan.
The relevant inquiry is not simply whether the category contained sufficient funding.
It is whether the funding could be accessed and translated into the support required.
The investigation should examine:
	•	The approved support purposes.
	•	The participant’s actual daily support requirements.
	•	Provider availability.
	•	Service agreements.
	•	Rosters and shift records.
	•	Cancelled or missed shifts.
	•	Support-worker attendance.
	•	Provider invoices.
	•	Claims made against the plan.
	•	Complaints about inadequate delivery.
	•	Corrective action taken after complaints.
Where a plan identifies substantial daily support needs, the evidence should establish whether those needs were met consistently.
The distinction between an allocation and a delivered service is especially important where the participant is dependent on support workers to obtain food, maintain accommodation, attend appointments or participate in the community.
An agency should not be treated as having fulfilled its practical responsibilities merely because money was allocated to a category.
220. Behaviour support and the risk of confusing disability support with behavioural control
The plan was previously recorded as allocating $27,958.80 to Behaviour Support.
Behaviour support should be examined in the context of the participant’s actual support needs, the relevant assessment and the applicable NDIS requirements.
The NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission⁠ provides regulatory information about behaviour support and regulated restrictive practices.
The investigation should distinguish:
	•	Positive behaviour support.
	•	Clinical treatment.
	•	Disability support.
	•	Risk management.
	•	Restrictive practices.
	•	Staff training.
	•	Incident response.
	•	Behaviour support plan implementation.
These are not interchangeable categories.
A behaviour support plan should not be used as a substitute for adequate accommodation, reliable staffing, ordinary daily assistance or the investigation of an external threat or incident.
Likewise, a person’s disagreement with a provider or their expression of distress should not automatically be treated as proof that the person requires more restrictive control.
Where restrictive practices are involved, the applicable authorisation, reporting, consent and oversight requirements must be examined.
Relevant records include:
	•	The original functional assessment.
	•	The behaviour support plan.
	•	Any interim plan.
	•	The comprehensive plan.
	•	Evidence of participant consultation.
	•	Provider training records.
	•	Restrictive-practice authorisations, if any.
	•	Incident reports.
	•	Implementation reviews.
	•	Complaints and corrective actions.
The archive identifies an interim behaviour support plan dated 15 March 2024. That record should be compared with subsequent plans and the participant’s circumstances at the time.
221. Improved Daily Living and the professional assessment record
The plan was previously recorded as allocating $11,140.53 to Improved Daily Living.
This category should be examined against the actual allied-health recommendations, assessments and services delivered.

	•	The assessment methods used.
	•	The functional limitations identified.
	•	The support needs documented.
	•	The recommended accommodation model.
	•	The recommended staffing arrangements.
	•	The rationale for the recommendations.
	•	Whether the participant was consulted.
	•	Whether the NDIA received the report.
	•	Whether the recommendations were accepted, modified or rejected.
	•	The reasons for any departure from the recommendations.
A professional recommendation is not automatically binding on the NDIA.
However, where a substantial recommendation is not adopted, the decision and its reasoning should be examined.
The question is whether the final plan was based on an adequate consideration of the participant’s needs and the available evidence.
222. Improved Living Arrangements: the significance of the approved amount
The plan was previously recorded as allocating $4,163.12 to Improved Living Arrangements.
The amount alone does not reveal what practical assistance was approved or delivered.
The original plan and associated correspondence should be examined to determine:

	•	Whether suitable providers were available.
	•	Whether the service was engaged.
	•	Whether the support was delivered.
	•	Whether the amount was sufficient for the intended task.
	•	Whether housing needs remained unresolved.
The participant’s housing situation should be considered alongside the support plan, not in isolation.
Where a person requires a particular accommodation model to live safely and independently, the availability of an assessment budget does not establish that the accommodation itself has been secured.
223. Support coordination and psychosocial recovery coaching
The plan was previously recorded as allocating $47,635 to Support Coordination and Psychosocial Recovery Coaches.
These supports can be important in helping participants navigate services, implement plans, coordinate providers and address barriers to participation.
The investigation should examine whether the support was actually delivered and whether it achieved its intended purpose.
Relevant evidence includes:
	•	The support coordination agreement.
	•	The recovery coaching agreement.
	•	The coordinator’s case notes.
	•	Participant contact records.
	•	Referrals.
	•	Provider communications.

	•	Complaints and responses.
	•	Changes of coordinator.
