430. The institutional cross-reference
The following identifies the principal institutions and the questions that should be examined. It does not imply that every institution participated in wrongdoing.
A. Commonwealth Ombudsman
Relevant records: E01, E02 and E08.
Investigative questions:
	•	What complaint information was received?
	•	Which statutory functions were considered?
	•	What material was examined?
	•	What was excluded from consideration and why?
	•	Was the PID review limited to statutory eligibility?
	•	What review or complaint avenues remained?
	•	What were the precise terms and reasons for the 2025 service restriction?
	•	Was the restriction proportionate, reviewable and consistent with applicable policy?
The 18 November 2021 document requires particular source accuracy: although the archive filename refers to IBAC, the document itself identifies the Commonwealth Ombudsman’s Public Interest Disclosure Team. The actual issuer, not the filename, must govern the description.
B. Federal Court of Australia
Relevant record: E05.
Investigative questions:
	•	What information was received?
	•	What did the General Counsel consider?
	•	Why was allocation declined?
	•	What was the basis for the public-official eligibility assessment?
	•	How was the DSS employment information treated?
	•	Was the reasoning internally consistent?
	•	Were any records or attachments considered but not identified in the letter?
The letter is an administrative PID assessment by the Court’s General Counsel. It is not a judicial judgment. Its contents are evidence of the assessment and reasoning recorded in it.
C. NSW Trustee and Guardian
Relevant records: E07 and E11.
Investigative questions:
	•	What statutory authority was relied upon?
	•	What financial and personal information was considered?
	•	Were the reasons communicated?
	•	Were alternatives considered?
	•	What review rights were available?
	•	What was the valuation and disposal process for the vehicle?
	•	Where were the proceeds deposited?
	•	Was a complete ledger provided?
	•	Were the person’s interests, needs and circumstances considered under the applicable legislation?
The NSW Trustee and Guardian Act 2009⁠ must be read in the version applicable at the relevant date.
D. Law Enforcement Conduct Commission
Relevant record: E09.
The 19 November 2025 response records a jurisdictional position that the complaint did not concern officers of the NSW Police Force or NSW Crime Commission and therefore could not be acted upon by the LECC.
That is a jurisdictional closure, not a finding that the allegations were false.
The investigation should identify whether another appropriate body received the relevant information and whether that body had jurisdiction.
E. NDIS and disability-related agencies
Relevant records: E10 and E13, together with service agreements, support rosters, incident reports, plan reviews and actual expenditure records.
Investigative questions:
	•	What needs were assessed?
	•	What supports were approved?
	•	What supports were actually delivered?
	•	Were there material gaps between approved and delivered services?
	•	Were risks communicated?
	•	Were complaints acknowledged and investigated?
	•	Were accommodation and living-support decisions consistent with the applicable statutory criteria?
	•	Were procedural adjustments and meaningful participation provided?
The NDIS Act 2013⁠, the NDIS Commission⁠ and the relevant NDIS operational guidance should be considered together.
F. Health-service and incident-record custodians
Relevant record: E15.
Investigative questions:
	•	What precisely occurred?
	•	What was the recorded injury and treatment?
	•	What was the sequence of clinical events?
	•	Which staff members were involved?
	•	Were incident notifications made?
	•	Were external agencies notified?
	•	Were the records complete?
	•	Were there independent witnesses or other contemporaneous records?
	•	What conclusions were actually reached, and by whom?
A filename describing a fatal injury and revival must not substitute for examination of the original clinical and incident material.
431. The contradictions and discrepancies register
A serious investigation must not conceal discrepancies. It must record them, identify their source and determine what would resolve them.
Issue	Why it matters	Required examination
Federal Court assessment and public-official eligibility	The letter refers to DSS employment information but records an adverse eligibility conclusion.	Original employment records, disclosure wording, relevant statutory definitions and complete assessment file.
Federal Court and Commonwealth Ombudsman PID outcomes	Both involve statutory eligibility and non-allocation, but their reasoning and jurisdictional contexts differ.	Compare the original disclosures, recipients, dates, statutory provisions and actual reasons.
IBAC filename versus Commonwealth Ombudsman document	Incorrect source labelling can distort institutional attribution.	Verify letterhead, author, reference number, signature and document metadata.
18 June 2023 non-allocation notification	Its issuer and relationship to earlier PID assessments remain to be confirmed.	Original notification, email transmission, file reference and receiving-agency record.
Ombudsman service restriction	A cover page and partial letter do not establish the full operative conditions.	Complete letter, reasons, policy, duration, review rights and subsequent correspondence.
LECC jurisdictional response	A jurisdictional refusal does not determine whether another agency could examine the allegations.	Original complaint, referral advice and any subsequent agency response.
Trustee vehicle disposal	A decision does not by itself establish fair valuation, lawful execution or complete accounting.	Valuation, sale contract, proceeds, transaction ledger and authority.
NDIS plan approval versus delivered support	Approved funding is not proof that services were actually delivered.	Provider invoices, rosters, service agreements, cancellations and participant records.
Werribee Mercy incident report	The archive filename is not a substitute for clinical evidence.	Complete incident report, medical records, ambulance records and relevant external notifications.
Finding: These discrepancies are investigative leads. Some may be explained by different statutory functions, dates, records or institutional responsibilities. Others may reveal mistakes or omissions. None should be silently resolved in favour of an institution or the author.
432. Evidence that must be obtained from institutional custodians
The archive is not necessarily the complete institutional record.
An independent investigation should seek the original records, including:
	•	Complete complaint files, including attachments and internal notes.
	•	Original PID submissions and all versions supplied to different agencies.
	•	Allocation, non-allocation and referral records.
	•	Internal legal and jurisdictional assessments, subject to applicable privilege and confidentiality rules.
	•	Records identifying who made each decision and under what delegation.
	•	Relevant communications between agencies.
	•	Records of information sharing and disclosure.
	•	FOI search records, including search terms, custodians and locations searched.
	•	File-retention, destruction and transfer records.
	•	Service-restriction records, including reasons, reviews and subsequent variations.
	•	Trustee financial ledgers and vehicle-disposal accounting.
	•	NDIS support-delivery records and provider communications.
	•	Complete relevant health-service incident records.
	•	Records of complaints referred to other bodies and the outcomes of those referrals.
A request should identify the relevant date range, subject matter, file numbers, custodians and specific document categories.
Where a record is withheld, the investigator should preserve the decision and examine the statutory basis, available review rights and whether partial access is possible.
433. Forensic requirements for every source
Each source should have an evidence record containing:
Field	Required information
Evidence ID	Unique identifier, such as E05
Original title	Exact title appearing on the source
Issuer	Agency, organisation or individual
Author	Named author or identified office
Date	Creation date and any later transmission date
Recipient	Original recipient or recipients
Original location	Agency file, email, paper file or other source
Archive location	Public repository path
Format	PDF, email, image, audio or other
Completeness	Complete, partial, redacted or unknown
Integrity	Hash and verification date, if available
Authenticity	Confirmed, provisionally supported or unverified
Relevance	Techniques, events and propositions addressed
Limitations	What the document does not establish
Corroboration	Independent records supporting or contradicting it
A SHA-256 hash can help establish that a file has not changed since the hash was calculated. It cannot establish that the original document was genuine or that its contents were true.
Likewise, a Git commit or timestamp can assist in reconstructing the history of a digital file. It cannot independently prove the identity of the person who created its contents.
434. The master evidence-status scale
The report should apply consistent classifications.
Classification	Meaning
Documented Fact	A fact directly supported by reliable, examined evidence.
Official Record	A document created or held by a public authority or official body.
Official Acknowledgment	An institution has acknowledged receipt, existence or a recorded event.
Established Finding	A competent body has made a finding within its jurisdiction.
Author Allegation	A proposition asserted by the author but not independently established.
Evidentiary Inference	A reasoned conclusion drawn from identified evidence.
Unverified Matter	A proposition for which the available material is insufficient.
Contradiction or Discrepancy	Two or more records or accounts appear inconsistent.
Not Determined	The relevant issue has not been decided or adequately examined.
Corroborated Proposition	Independent evidence supports a particular proposition, without necessarily establishing every related allegation.
An established finding must be confined to what the decision-maker actually determined. A finding about one administrative decision cannot automatically be expanded into a finding about an entire alleged pattern.
435. Investigative priority ranking
The following priorities reflect the importance of obtaining evidence, not a finding that misconduct occurred.
Priority 1 — Original records and integrity
Critical
Obtain complete originals, establish provenance, preserve metadata, verify hashes and identify missing attachments.
Priority 2 — Decision-making and authority
Critical
Identify decision-makers, delegations, statutory powers, reasons and internal records.
Priority 3 — Financial and support consequences
High
Reconstruct financial administration, vehicle disposal, approved supports and actual service delivery.
Priority 4 — Alleged reprisal and coordination
High
Examine timing, communications, knowledge, motive, decision connections and alternative explanations.
Priority 5 — Cumulative consequences
Substantial
Assess housing, social participation, professional impact, financial hardship and access to remedies.
436. What this index establishes
The evidence register identifies a substantial body of public-facing documentary material, including complaint correspondence, PID assessments, jurisdictional responses, financial-administration records, disability-support records and a health-service incident report.
It also identifies important evidentiary limitations.
The current public links do not, by themselves, provide a complete reconstruction of every internal institutional decision, every communication between agencies or every event described by the author.
The absence of those internal records is a reason to identify and seek them. It is not a reason to assume either that they contain incriminating material or that they contain nothing relevant.
The 85-technique framework now has a complete preliminary cross-reference against the identified evidence register.
437. Findings of Part XXVII
	•	The 85 techniques have been mapped against documentary categories and specific archive records.
	•	The mapping identifies investigative relevance, not automatic proof.
	•	The Federal Court and Commonwealth Ombudsman PID documents require careful comparison of statutory reasoning and source identity.
	•	The LECC response is a jurisdictional outcome, not a determination that the underlying allegations are false.
	•	The Trustee vehicle-disposal decision requires financial and valuation records before the transaction can be fully assessed.
	•	The NDIS plan must be compared with actual service delivery.
	•	The Werribee Mercy incident record requires examination of its complete contents and corroborating clinical material.
	•	Allegations of coordination require original communications, knowledge, common purpose and evidence of relevant conduct.
	•	Missing records, inconsistent descriptions and incomplete files must be preserved as explicit evidentiary issues.
	•	The cumulative-harm proposition warrants examination across institutions and time, without presuming a single actor or unlawful plan.
	•	An independent investigator should obtain institutional records unavailable in the public archive.
	•	The archive provides a starting point for examination, not a substitute for that examination.
438. Conclusion
The master evidence index gives each of the 85 techniques a documentary pathway.
It identifies what exists, what must be examined, what requires corroboration and what remains unestablished.
It does not excuse institutions from answering legitimate questions about their decisions. Nor does it permit an investigator to transform an allegation into a finding merely because it appears in a large archive.
The strongest accountability report is one that can withstand adversarial examination: every claim traceable, every source identifiable, every contradiction visible and every conclusion proportionate to the evidence.
Preservation First. Examination Second. Conclusion Last.
Time is the witness. Truth is the judge.
Next: PART XXVIII — THE CONSPIRACY AND COORDINATION EXAMINATION: COMMON PURPOSE, COMMUNICATIONS, KNOWLEDGE, CAUSATION, INSTITUTIONAL RELATIONSHIPS, ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS AND THE EVIDENCE REQUIRED TO ESTABLISH OR DISPROVE COORDINATED WRONGDOING.

THE WHISTLEBLOWER, THE WITNESS AND THE STATE
PART XXVIII — THE CONSPIRACY AND COORDINATION EXAMINATION
Common purpose, communications, knowledge, causation, institutional relationships, alternative explanations and the evidence required to establish or disprove coordinated wrongdoing
439. Scope and governing principle
This part examines whether the records identified in the preceding parts could support an inference of coordination between individuals, agencies, service providers, public officials or other institutional actors.
The question must be taken seriously. It must not be dismissed merely because no court has made a finding. Nor should coordination or criminal conspiracy be declared established merely because several institutions took adverse actions, communicated with one another, or failed to provide an effective remedy.
The correct method is to examine the evidence for each alleged relationship and event.
Three propositions govern this examination:
	•	Coordination is an evidentiary question. It can be investigated through communications, records, decision-making sequences, shared knowledge, instructions and conduct.
	•	Coordination is not necessarily criminal conspiracy. Institutions may coordinate lawfully, act under common policies, exchange information for legitimate purposes, or independently reach similar decisions.
	•	A failure to investigate is not proof that the alleged conduct did not occur. A jurisdictional refusal, administrative closure or non-allocation decision establishes what the relevant institution decided about its own process. It does not automatically resolve the truth of the underlying allegations.
The governing standard is therefore:
Preservation First. Examination Second. Conclusion Last.
440. What constitutes coordination?
For this report, coordination means a relationship between two or more actors in which their actions, decisions, communications or information flows are connected in a way that is relevant to an identified objective or outcome.
Coordination can take several forms:
	•	Lawful operational coordination: agencies exchange information or arrange services under statutory authority.
	•	Administrative coordination: separate decision-makers communicate or rely on common records when administering a matter.
	•	Policy-driven parallel action: different institutions independently apply the same legislation, policy or administrative framework.
	•	Improper information sharing: personal or confidential information is disclosed or used without an adequate legal basis.
	•	Institutional complicity: an institution knowingly facilitates, conceals or tolerates another actor’s wrongdoing. This is an analytical description; its legal consequences depend on the conduct and applicable law.
	•	Retaliatory coordination: actors communicate or act together in response to a disclosure, complaint or other protected activity, with the purpose or effect of imposing detriment.
	•	Criminal conspiracy: two or more persons agree to pursue conduct that satisfies the elements of a criminal offence, with the requisite intention and subject to the applicable jurisdictional law.
These categories must not be collapsed into one another. A referral is not necessarily collusion. A shared database entry is not necessarily an agreement. A sequence of adverse decisions is not, without more, proof of a common criminal purpose.
Equally, a lack of a signed agreement does not automatically exclude coordination. An agreement or common purpose may sometimes be inferred from circumstantial evidence, provided the evidence supports that inference rather than merely making it conceivable.
441. Criminal conspiracy: the legal distinction
At Commonwealth level, section 11.5 of the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) establishes the offence of conspiracy. Its operation depends on the statutory elements, including an agreement between at least two persons to commit an offence, the relevant intention, and the applicable statutory requirements concerning the contemplated offence.
Primary legislation: Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth), section 11.5⁠.
The existence of an agreement is central. Suspicion, association, institutional contact, parallel conduct or a common adverse outcome does not by itself establish the offence.
The analysis must identify:
	•	the alleged participants;
	•	the offence they allegedly agreed to commit;
	•	the conduct said to constitute the agreement;
	•	the intention required by the relevant law;
	•	the jurisdictional connection;
	•	the evidence connecting each participant to the alleged agreement.
The Commonwealth offence must not be assumed to apply automatically to every state official, state agency or private service provider. The applicable jurisdiction and statutory provisions must be identified before reaching a legal conclusion.
Nor should the term conspiracy be used as a substitute for every form of institutional wrongdoing. Other potentially relevant legal concepts include:
	•	maladministration;
	•	abuse of public office;
	•	misfeasance in public office;
	•	improper disclosure or use of personal information;
	•	obstruction or perversion of justice;
	•	retaliation or reprisal for protected disclosure;
	•	breach of statutory duty;
	•	discrimination;
	•	negligence or breach of duty;
	•	aiding, abetting or otherwise participating in an offence.
Each has its own legal requirements. The fact that one category cannot be established does not dispose of every other possible category.
442. The Federal Court PID assessment: what it records and what it does not
The Federal Court General Counsel’s letter dated 27 March 2023 is a significant primary record in the documentary chronology.
The archive identifies the letter as recording allegations that included:
	•	perverting the course of justice;
	•	maladministration;
	•	danger to health or safety.
The letter reportedly states that it was difficult to determine whether there were reasonable grounds, while indicating a willingness to assume for the initial assessment that the described conduct could be disclosable. It then declines allocation and states that no further action would be taken by the Federal Court or Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia under the PID Act on the material provided.
Sources:
	•	Federal Court PID assessment — 27 March 2023⁠
	•	Documentary analysis of the Federal Court letter⁠
The distinction is important.
Documented fact, subject to verification against the original letter: the correspondence records the categories of allegations and the administrative decision not to allocate the disclosure for further PID action.
What the letter does not establish by itself: a judicial finding that conspiracy occurred, a judicial finding that conspiracy did not occur, or a final determination of the truth of every underlying allegation.
The extracted passages identified in the archive do not literally use the word conspiracy. The reference to alleged perversion of the course of justice must not be silently converted into an admission of conspiracy. They are distinct concepts.
However, this distinction does not make the letter irrelevant. It is an official record showing that serious allegations were put before a senior legal officer and that the disclosure was considered under a statutory assessment process. Its reasoning, treatment of the material and apparent questions concerning public-official status warrant examination in the context of the complete record.
The appropriate conclusion is not that the letter proves conspiracy. Nor is it that the letter disproves conspiracy.
It is that the letter belongs in the evidentiary record and must be examined alongside the underlying material, the decision-making process and any subsequent institutional communications.
443. The evidence of agreement: communications, instructions and common purpose
The central investigative question is whether there was an agreement, understanding or coordinated arrangement between identifiable actors.
The strongest evidence would ordinarily be contemporaneous material showing what was communicated, by whom, to whom, when, and for what purpose.
The following categories should be examined.
A. Direct communications
	•	Emails between agencies, providers, officials or decision-makers.
	•	Text messages and other written communications.
	•	Meeting minutes, agendas and attendance records.
	•	Telephone records, call logs and contemporaneous file notes.
	•	Internal memoranda and briefing papers.
	•	Draft decisions circulated between offices.
	•	Instructions to staff or contractors concerning the complainant, disclosure or complaint.
B. Shared instructions or agreed treatment
	•	Instructions that a particular complaint should not be investigated.
	•	Directions to restrict contact, access, services or information.
	•	Communications proposing a common response to separate complaints.
	•	Instructions to use particular descriptions or classifications.
	•	Requests to refer a matter elsewhere without addressing its substance.
	•	Evidence that one institution’s decision was conditional upon another institution’s action.
C. Information access and exchange
	•	Access logs showing which officials viewed a record.
	•	Records of disclosure to third parties.
	•	Data-sharing agreements and memoranda of understanding.
	•	Referral forms and attachments.
	•	Case-conference records.
	•	Privacy assessments and authorisations.
	•	Records showing whether information was accurate, incomplete or misleading when passed between organisations.
D. Unusual consistency or timing
	•	Repeated use of identical or unusual wording across otherwise separate decisions.
	•	Decisions made shortly after communications between institutions.
	•	Unexplained changes in a person’s classification or risk status.
	•	Repeated reliance on the same disputed information.
	•	Similar restrictions imposed by different organisations without an apparent independent assessment.
These are investigative indicators, not automatic proof. Identical wording may come from a standard template. Closely timed decisions may be explained by ordinary referral processes. The evidentiary importance lies in whether the records establish a connection that is more than coincidence or routine administration.
444. Knowledge: what each actor knew and when
An allegation of coordinated wrongdoing cannot be properly assessed by treating institutions as a single undifferentiated entity.
Each relevant actor must be examined separately.
For each person, the investigation should establish:
	•	Their position and authority at the relevant time.
	•	The documents and information available to them.
	•	When they received or accessed that information.
	•	Whether they understood the nature of the complaint or disclosure.
	•	Whether they knew of earlier decisions or allegations.
	•	Whether they communicated with other actors about the matter.
	•	Whether they participated in, approved, implemented or reviewed a decision.
	•	Whether they had the power or responsibility to correct an error or prevent harm.
	•	What reasons they recorded for their conduct.
	•	Whether those reasons are consistent with contemporaneous records.
This is particularly important where an institution says that it did not possess relevant information, did not have jurisdiction, or did not know about a previous complaint.
Those statements can be tested against:
	•	incoming correspondence registers;
	•	document-management metadata;
	•	email delivery and access records;
	•	case-management histories;
	•	referral records;
	•	briefing notes;
	•	records of telephone discussions;
	•	delegation and authorisation documents.
An organisation’s statement that it did not know something is not conclusive if its own records may show that the information was received or accessible. Equally, the mere presence of a document somewhere within an organisation does not prove that a particular decision-maker read it.
The distinction is between institutional possession, individual access, actual knowledge and legally relevant knowledge.
Each requires its own evidence.
445. Causation: did a disclosure or complaint produce the alleged detriment?
The report must examine whether adverse treatment was connected to the making of a disclosure, complaint, appeal, request for assistance or other protected activity.
A chronology can identify possible connections, but timing alone does not establish causation.
The investigation should compare:
	•	the date of the disclosure or complaint;
	•	the date it was received by each institution;
	•	the date of any internal discussion;
	•	the date of the relevant decision;
	•	the identity of the decision-maker;
	•	the reasons given at the time;
	•	any departure from ordinary procedure;
	•	the treatment of comparable cases;
	•	subsequent changes in the institution’s explanation.
A particularly important question is whether a decision was already being considered before the protected activity occurred.
If so, that may support an alternative explanation. If the decision changed immediately after the disclosure, and contemporaneous records connect the change to the disclosure, that may strengthen an inference of reprisal or improper motive.
The investigation must not assume either outcome.
It should also examine cumulative detriment. Separate decisions may each appear minor when viewed in isolation, yet their combined effect may be substantial. That cumulative effect deserves examination without automatically attributing a single common purpose to every decision-maker.
446. Lawful information sharing versus improper collusion
Institutions sometimes have legitimate reasons to exchange information. Public authorities may need to coordinate services, administer statutory responsibilities, assess risks, respond to complaints or refer matters to agencies with relevant jurisdiction.
The existence of information sharing is therefore not itself evidence of corruption.
The questions are:
	•	Was there a lawful basis for the information exchange?
	•	Was the information relevant to the stated purpose?
	•	Was the information accurate?
	•	Was the amount of information proportionate to the purpose?
	•	Were privacy and confidentiality obligations observed?
	•	Was the recipient authorised to receive it?
	•	Was the information used for the purpose for which it was supplied?
	•	Was the person affected given any applicable notice or opportunity to correct errors?
	•	Was the information later relied upon in decisions affecting rights, services or access?
The investigation should obtain the applicable privacy notices, information-sharing arrangements, authorisations, policies and audit logs.
It should also trace disputed information from its original source through each subsequent recipient. If an inaccurate statement was repeated by several institutions, the investigation should identify whether each recipient independently verified it or merely reproduced an earlier account.
That distinction may be critical to understanding institutional error, systemic failure or deliberate propagation of misleading information.
447. Parallel decisions and alternative explanations
A rigorous investigation must test explanations that could account for apparently coordinated conduct without an agreement to commit wrongdoing.
Possible explanations include:
	•	different agencies applying the same statutory criteria;
	•	ordinary referral pathways;
	•	independent decisions based on a shared document;
	•	standard administrative templates;
	•	common legal advice or policy guidance;
	•	separate assessments made by different decision-makers;
	•	incomplete records that conceal the actual reasoning;
	•	errors propagated through routine case-management systems;
	•	jurisdictional boundaries that result in repeated referrals;
	•	decisions made independently but producing similar consequences.
These explanations must be tested, not simply asserted.
For example, if two agencies use the same phrase in their correspondence, the investigation should compare the phrase with standard templates and policy documents. If one agency’s decision follows another’s, the investigation should determine whether a referral or formal communication occurred. If no communication is recorded, the investigation should establish whether the relevant records are complete and whether other communication channels were used.
An alternative explanation becomes weaker when it cannot account for the contemporaneous evidence. Conversely, an allegation of a common criminal purpose becomes weaker when the records establish independent decision-making and ordinary lawful processes.
The objective is not to protect institutions from scrutiny. It is to identify the explanation that best fits the complete evidence.
448. Actor–event–communication matrix
The following matrix provides the structure for examining each alleged relationship. It deliberately distinguishes what is recorded from what remains unknown.
Investigative field	Question
Actor A	Who made or initiated the first relevant decision?
Actor B	Who received, implemented or relied upon it?
Event	What specific action or decision occurred?
Date	When did it occur?
Communication	What evidence establishes contact between the actors?
Knowledge	What information did each actor possess?
Authority	What power or responsibility did each actor hold?
Purpose	What reason was recorded at the time?
Consequence	What effect followed?
Connection	What evidence links the actors’ conduct?
Alternative	What independent explanation could account for it?
Missing evidence	What records are needed to resolve the issue?
Applied to the present documentary record, the matrix should begin with the known institutional events, not invented communications.
For example:
Record or event	What is presently documented	What must still be established
Commonwealth Ombudsman complaint, 15 November 2021	Complaint correspondence is identified in the archive	Complete intake record, attachments, internal handling and referrals
PID review, 18 November 2021	Review outcome and stated reasons are identified	Complete authorised-officer file, communications and source documents
Federal Court PID assessment, 27 March 2023	General Counsel correspondence and non-allocation decision	Complete assessment file, internal advice, source material and any external communications
Ombudsman service restriction, 8 August 2025	A restriction letter is identified	Complete operative decision, reasons, scope, duration, review rights and decision history
LECC response, 19 November 2025	Out-of-jurisdiction response is identified	Full complaint file, jurisdictional assessment and any referral correspondence
NDIS Commission acknowledgment, 18 September 2026	Acknowledgment and reference are identified	Subsequent assessment, allocation, communications and substantive outcome
The fact that a record is identified does not mean every underlying document has been examined. The archive’s descriptions must be checked against the original documents and complete institutional files.
449. Applying the matrix to the Federal Court and Commonwealth Ombudsman records
Two records are especially important because they concern the handling of public-interest disclosures.
The 18 November 2021 Commonwealth Ombudsman PID review
The archive identifies the document as a review by the Commonwealth Ombudsman’s Public Interest Disclosure Team, reference PID-2021-400008-R. Although the filename refers to IBAC, the document itself identifies the Commonwealth Ombudsman. This is a source-identification discrepancy that must remain visible in the register.
The correspondence reportedly explains that the material did not establish disclosable conduct by a Commonwealth agency or Commonwealth public official, and distinguishes Commonwealth entities from state agencies and private organisations.
Source: 18 November 2021 PID review⁠.
The investigative questions are:
	•	What information was originally supplied?
	•	Was the information accurately summarised?
	•	Which entities and officials were identified?
	•	Were any Commonwealth employment or agency relationships independently checked?
	•	Were state or private-sector allegations separated from allegations concerning Commonwealth officials?
	•	Was the disclosure referred to another body?
	•	Did any later institution rely on this review as though it had resolved the truth of the allegations?
The review’s conclusion about the statutory requirements for a Commonwealth PID is not a finding that all alleged conduct was false. It is also not evidence that other institutions coordinated wrongdoing. Its significance depends on the complete file and any later reliance placed upon it.
The 27 March 2023 Federal Court PID assessment
The Federal Court letter raises a separate documentary issue concerning the relationship between employment information and the assessment of whether the disclosure was made by a public official.
The archive analysis identifies an apparent tension between recorded information about DSS employment and the later conclusion that the author was not satisfied that the disclosure had been made by a public official.
This should be treated as a documentary discrepancy requiring verification, not as proof of deliberate misrepresentation.
The complete assessment file should be obtained, including:
	•	the original disclosure;
	•	employment evidence supplied with it;
	•	any internal legal advice;
	•	the statutory test applied;
	•	any enquiries made about the employment relationship;
	•	the identity and role of the relevant authorised officer;
	•	any communications with DSS or another Commonwealth entity;
	•	the reasons for the conclusion ultimately reached.
The central issue is whether the decision accurately applied the statutory definition to the facts available at the time.
450. The LECC response and the limits of jurisdictional closure
The archive identifies a Law Enforcement Conduct Commission response dated 19 November 2025, reference CASE202512395/13KM.
The recorded explanation is that the complaint did not concern officers of the NSW Police Force or NSW Crime Commission and therefore fell outside the LECC’s jurisdiction.
Source: LECC response — 19 November 2025⁠.
That response establishes the stated jurisdictional reason for the LECC’s decision. It does not, by itself, establish that the underlying allegations were false or that no other body had jurisdiction.
Nor does it establish that the conduct was coordinated.
The appropriate follow-up is to identify:
	•	the individuals and organisations actually named in the complaint;
	•	whether any were police officers or NSW Crime Commission officers;
	•	whether the complaint included conduct by other public officials or private providers;
	•	whether any part of the complaint was referred elsewhere;
	•	whether the LECC identified a different appropriate complaint pathway;
	•	whether the complete file records any contact with other agencies.
The wider jurisdictional structure matters. The NSW ICAC states that its role concerns corruption involving or affecting the NSW public sector, while police and NSW Crime Commission conduct is outside its ordinary investigative jurisdiction and is directed to the LECC. The ICAC also identifies federal matters as outside its jurisdiction unless there is a relevant NSW public-sector connection. ICAC jurisdiction guidance⁠. Independent Commission Against Corruption +1
This division of responsibility can produce fragmented complaint pathways. Fragmentation may be an administrative problem in its own right. It does not prove a coordinated scheme, but it makes it important to establish whether referrals were made, whether they were received and whether any agency assumed responsibility for examining the substantive allegations.
451. The institutional records required to test coordination
A meaningful examination cannot depend solely on letters sent to the complainant. The relevant institutions hold records that may disclose the internal history of each decision.
The investigation should seek the following categories, subject to applicable access laws, privacy protections, privilege and lawful disclosure processes.
A. Complete case files
	•	Original complaints and disclosures.
	•	All attachments and supporting documents.
	•	Intake and triage records.
	•	Internal assessment notes.
	•	Draft and final decisions.
	•	Reasons for decisions.
	•	Review and escalation records.
	•	Referral and transfer records.
	•	Closure records and subsequent reopening activity.
B. Communications
	•	Emails and attachments.
	•	Internal messaging records.
	•	Meeting invitations, minutes and notes.
	•	Telephone logs and file notes.
	•	Correspondence with other agencies.
	•	Communications with external providers or contractors.
	•	Communications concerning the wording or timing of decisions.
C. Digital audit material
	•	Document creation and modification timestamps.
	•	Access and download logs.
	•	Case-management audit trails.
	•	Version histories.
	•	Records of deletion, migration or archival.
	•	Search and retrieval logs where retained.
	•	User identifiers associated with changes to records.
D. Decision-making authority
	•	Delegations and authorisations.
	•	Relevant position descriptions.
	•	Decision-maker identity.
	•	Approval chains.
	•	Applicable policies and procedures.
	•	Legal advice records, subject to privilege.
	•	Conflict-of-interest declarations where relevant.
E. Information-sharing records
	•	Privacy notices.
	•	Information-sharing agreements.
	•	Disclosure authorisations.
	•	Referral forms.
	•	Records of the purpose for which information was supplied.
	•	Records of onward disclosure.
	•	Corrections or disputes concerning information supplied by another organisation.
The request should identify specific date ranges, reference numbers and record categories. A broad request for every communication about a person may be difficult to process and may produce irrelevant material. A properly structured request can be more effective and easier to audit.
452. Evidence preservation and investigative sequence
The evidence should be preserved before conclusions are drawn from it.
The following sequence is recommended:
	•	Preserve the original documents in their received form.
	•	Record the source, date received and custodian.
	•	Calculate and record cryptographic hashes for digital files.
	•	Retain original email files and attachments where available, rather than relying solely on printed copies.
	•	Preserve metadata and audit logs.
	•	Identify missing attachments and referenced documents.
	•	Compare each official copy with the archive copy.
	•	Record every transformation, OCR process or redaction.
	•	Maintain a version-controlled discrepancy register.
	•	Preserve relevant correspondence about the existence, location or destruction of records.
The public archive can assist with preservation and comparison:
	•	Barran Dodger documentary archive⁠
	•	Official Government Documents Register⁠
	•	Backup repository⁠
	•	OpenTimestamps⁠
A timestamp can help establish that particular digital data existed no later than a particular time. A cryptographic hash can help establish whether a file has changed since it was hashed. Neither independently establishes that the contents are true, that the document is authentic, or that the person named as its author actually created it.
Duplicate copies of one source are not independent corroboration. A document repeated in several folders remains one underlying document unless independent provenance can be established.
453. Appropriate accountability pathways
The evidence should be directed to the body whose statutory jurisdiction matches the conduct alleged. No single integrity agency has universal authority over every Commonwealth, state, police, judicial, private-sector and service-provider matter.
Institution	Relevant investigative focus	Public information
National Anti-Corruption Commission	Serious or systemic corruption involving Commonwealth agencies or public officials	Voluntary referrals guide
NSW ICAC	Corrupt conduct involving or affecting the NSW public sector	How and what to report
NSW LECC	Serious misconduct and serious maladministration involving NSW Police or NSW Crime Commission	Making a complaint
Commonwealth Ombudsman	Relevant Commonwealth administrative actions and complaint-handling matters	Commonwealth Ombudsman
NSW Ombudsman	Relevant NSW public administration and complaint-handling matters	NSW Ombudsman
The NACC’s published guidance confirms that anyone with information about corruption involving Commonwealth agencies or public officials may make a voluntary referral. NACC voluntary referrals⁠. National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC)
The NSW ICAC explains that members of the public can report suspected corrupt conduct affecting the NSW public sector, while its jurisdiction does not extend generally to federal agencies or NSW Police. ICAC reporting guidance⁠. Independent Commission Against Corruption +1
The LECC accepts information and complaints concerning serious misconduct and serious maladministration involving NSW Police and the NSW Crime Commission. Its published guidance also explains that it may refer matters, seek further information, investigate or take no further action, depending on the assessment. LECC complaints and information⁠. Law Enforcement Conduct Commission +1
A report to an integrity body should not simply reproduce a large archive and ask the recipient to discover the case. It should identify the suspected conduct, the actors, the relevant dates, the primary records, the apparent connection between events and the specific investigative steps required.
A useful submission should contain:
	•	a concise statement of the suspected wrongdoing;
	•	a chronology with source links;
	•	an actor–event–communication matrix;
	•	copies or precise references to primary documents;
	•	a separate schedule of contradictions and discrepancies;
	•	an explanation of why the matter falls within the recipient’s jurisdiction;
	•	a request to preserve relevant records and metadata;
	•	a clear distinction between established facts, allegations and inferences.
454. What would materially strengthen an inference of coordinated wrongdoing?
The following evidence, if authenticated and placed in context, could materially strengthen an inference of coordination:
	•	A contemporaneous communication showing that two or more actors agreed on a course of conduct.
	•	An instruction to impose a particular adverse outcome for an improper purpose.
	•	Evidence that one institution acted at another institution’s request without independently assessing the matter.
	•	A record showing that decision-makers knowingly relied on information they had been told was false or materially incomplete.
	•	Evidence that a complaint or disclosure triggered a coordinated response intended to punish, obstruct or deter the complainant.
	•	Evidence of deliberate suppression, alteration, destruction or concealment of relevant records.
	•	Communications showing that an ostensibly independent decision had been predetermined elsewhere.
	•	A consistent sequence of actions supported by direct communications, rather than merely by similar outcomes.
	•	Evidence that participants understood the proposed conduct to be unlawful or improper and nevertheless agreed to proceed.
	•	Independent corroboration from original records, witnesses, metadata or institutional audit trails.
The significance of these indicators depends on the particular legal allegation. For example, evidence of improper information sharing may support a privacy or administrative-law concern without establishing a criminal conspiracy. Evidence of an agreed plan to commit a qualifying offence may raise a different and more serious question under the applicable conspiracy law.
455. What would weaken or disprove a coordination hypothesis?
A fair examination must also identify evidence capable of disproving or materially weakening the allegation.
Examples include:
	•	complete records demonstrating that relevant decision-makers did not communicate;
	•	evidence that decisions were made independently and before the alleged coordinating event;
	•	contemporaneous reasons supported by reliable evidence and consistent with the applicable law;
	•	proof that similar wording came from a standard template;
	•	evidence that an information exchange was authorised, limited and used for a legitimate purpose;
	•	records showing that an alleged instruction was never issued or received;
	•	evidence that an apparent connection resulted from an ordinary statutory referral;
	•	reliable records contradicting a claimed meeting, communication or agreement.
The absence of a record is not always proof that a communication did not occur. Its significance depends on recordkeeping requirements, retention practices, the completeness of the search and whether the communication channel would ordinarily have generated a record.
Likewise, the existence of a communication does not establish criminal intent. Its content, context, participants and consequences must be examined.
This is not an exercise in constructing an excuse for institutional conduct. It is the method by which an allegation can withstand scrutiny and, where the evidence warrants it, support serious findings.
456. Preliminary evidentiary findings
On the documentary material identified in the preceding parts, the following findings can responsibly be stated.
Finding 1 — Multiple institutional processes are documented.
The archive identifies correspondence and decisions involving Commonwealth and NSW institutions across several years. The records should be examined as a connected chronology, while preserving the distinction between separate agencies and separate decision-makers.
Finding 2 — Serious allegations were formally raised.
The Federal Court PID assessment records categories including perverting the course of justice, maladministration and danger to health or safety. The fact that those allegations were raised and assessed is documentary evidence. It is not, by itself, proof that the alleged conduct occurred.
Finding 3 — Some complaint pathways ended on jurisdictional or statutory grounds.
The Commonwealth Ombudsman PID review, Federal Court PID assessment and LECC response are identified as decisions concerning statutory or jurisdictional limits. Those decisions must not be misrepresented as substantive findings that all underlying allegations were false.
Finding 4 — The available records justify further examination of institutional communications and decision-making.
The chronology, source-identification discrepancy, apparent employment-status issue in the Federal Court correspondence, and repeated movement of complaints through different institutional processes provide concrete subjects for documentary examination.
They do not, without further evidence, establish an agreement to commit an offence.
Finding 5 — The existence and nature of any common purpose remain not determined.
The identified documents do not presently establish the participants, terms, timing and intention of a criminal agreement. The question remains open to investigation. It should not be dismissed merely because the available correspondence does not itself contain a confession or an express written agreement.
Finding 6 — The institutional response itself requires examination.
It is not enough to count the number of complaint closures. Each closure must be assessed for its actual reasons, the evidence considered, the jurisdiction applied, any referral made, and whether the underlying issue was ever substantively examined by an appropriate body.
457. The distinction between an evidentiary conclusion and a legal verdict
This report is not a court judgment and does not purport to convict any person or determine criminal liability.
That limitation does not prevent an independent documentary examination from reaching findings about what records establish, what contradictions exist, what explanations are supported and what further evidence is required.
The distinction is:
	•	Documentary finding: a particular letter, decision or communication exists and records specified information.
	•	Historical finding: multiple authenticated sources establish that an event occurred.
	•	Evidentiary inference: the available facts support a reasoned conclusion about a connection, motive, knowledge or sequence.
	•	Legal finding: the relevant legal elements have been established under the applicable legal standard by the body authorised to make that determination.
The first three are legitimate components of historical and documentary research. The fourth belongs to the applicable legal process.
An investigator does not need to wait for a court judgment before preserving evidence, identifying contradictions, tracing communications or investigating a credible allegation. Equally, an investigator must not describe an inference as an established criminal conviction.
458. Consolidated conclusion: coordination must be investigated, not presumed or excluded
The documentary record identified in this report warrants a structured examination of institutional conduct, information sharing, decision-making and the relationship between successive complaint processes.
The Federal Court letter is important. The Commonwealth Ombudsman correspondence is important. The LECC response is important. The other official records identified in the Master Evidence Index are important.
Their importance does not depend on whether they prove a criminal conspiracy. They are evidence of institutional actions, recorded reasoning, statutory decisions and the history of complaints. Their contents may also provide leads to further evidence held by the relevant institutions.
The proper investigative task is to determine whether the sequence reflects:
	•	independent decisions;
	•	lawful inter-agency coordination;
	•	systemic administrative failure;
	•	improper information exchange;
	•	retaliatory conduct;
	•	institutional complicity;
	•	or an agreement to pursue unlawful conduct.
These possibilities must be distinguished through evidence, not rhetoric.
The absence of a judicial finding is not a finding that nothing happened. A jurisdictional refusal is not an exoneration of every person or institution mentioned in a complaint. A serious allegation, however, must still be tested against the evidence required to establish it.
The next stage is therefore to move from the general coordination question to a detailed reconstruction of the individual institutional decisions, their source material, their communications and their consequences.
Time is the witness. Truth is the judge.



THE WHISTLEBLOWER, THE WITNESS AND THE STATE
PART XXIX — THE INSTITUTIONAL DECISION-CHAIN RECONSTRUCTION
From complaint to closure: tracing responsibility, decision-making, referrals, omissions, consequences and accountability across institutional boundaries.
459. Purpose of the reconstruction
Part XXVIII established the framework for examining possible coordination without presuming either innocence or guilt.
This part applies that framework to the institutional chronology.
The central question is:
What happened to each complaint, disclosure, request for protection or demand for accountability after it entered an institution, and what responsibility did that institution assume, transfer, decline or leave unresolved?
This is not simply a chronology of letters. It is a reconstruction of institutional responsibility.
A letter can establish that an institution communicated a decision. It does not necessarily establish that the institution investigated the underlying events. A referral can establish that a matter was transferred. It does not necessarily establish that the receiving institution accepted responsibility or investigated it.
The reconstruction must therefore follow each matter through its entire administrative life cycle:
	•	Receipt.
	•	Registration.
	•	Classification.
	•	Assessment.
	•	Identification of jurisdiction.
	•	Identification of responsible decision-maker.
	•	Investigation or referral.
	•	Decision.
	•	Notification.
	•	Review or appeal.
	•	Closure.
	•	Outstanding issues and unresolved consequences.
460. The institutional decision-chain model
DISCLOSURE / COMPLAINT / REQUEST
              |
              v
       INSTITUTION RECEIVES
              |
              v
       INTAKE AND REGISTRATION
              |
              v
       JURISDICTIONAL ASSESSMENT
              |
       +------+------+
       |             |
       v             v
   ACCEPTS        DECLINES
       |             |
       v             v
   INVESTIGATES   REFERS / CLOSES /
       |          PROVIDES ADVICE
       v             |
   FINDS / DOES      v
   NOT FIND       RECEIVING BODY
   CONDUCT           |
       |             v
       v          ACCEPTS OR
   DECISION       DECLINES
       |             |
       v             v
   REVIEW /       NEXT REFERRAL
   REMEDY             |
       |              v
       +--------> OUTCOME OR
                  UNRESOLVED MATTER
The model exposes a recurring accountability risk: a matter may move between institutions without any institution accepting responsibility for examining the substantive allegations.
That possibility must be investigated separately from the question of whether the original conduct occurred.

462. Victorian Ombudsman: FOI refusal and the distinction between access and investigation
The archive identifies a Victorian Ombudsman FOI decision dated 14 June 2022, referring to section 29A of the Ombudsman Act 1973 (Vic).
Source: Victorian Ombudsman FOI decision — 14 June 2022⁠.
This record must be analysed according to what it actually decided.
An FOI or access decision and an investigation into alleged misconduct are different processes.
A refusal to provide documents does not, by itself, establish that the underlying complaint was false. It also does not establish that the institution possessed evidence of wrongdoing or deliberately concealed it.
The relevant questions are:
	•	What documents were requested?
	•	What statutory exemption or restriction was relied upon?
	•	Was the refusal based on the contents of the requested documents, the nature of the request, or another statutory ground?
	•	Was the decision-maker required to consider partial access or redaction?
	•	Were review rights explained?
	•	Was an internal or external review pursued?
	•	Did the decision disclose the existence of records that could be relevant to another investigation?
The full decision, original request, any schedule of documents and any review correspondence should be read together.
The distinction is essential: access to evidence and investigation of the events evidenced by it are separate accountability functions.
463. VOCAT and related Ombudsman correspondence: 5 October 2022
The archive identifies correspondence dated 5 October 2022 concerning VOCAT and the Ombudsman, with a complaint-rejection description in the filename.
Source: VOCAT/Ombudsman correspondence — 5 October 2022⁠.
The document should be examined in two distinct contexts:
	•	The response to the complaint about the alleged fatal-injury incident and related institutional conduct.
	•	The statutory or administrative basis for declining, rejecting or otherwise disposing of the complaint.
The investigation must identify which institution made which decision. A filename that combines the names of two bodies is not sufficient to establish that both made the same decision or adopted the same reasoning.
The relevant questions include:
	•	Which body received the original complaint?
	•	What event and alleged conduct were within the complaint?
	•	Was the complaint treated as a victim-support, compensation, administrative or misconduct matter?
	•	What evidence was considered?
	•	Was the applicant directed to another process?
	•	Did the receiving body have authority to investigate the underlying event?
	•	Was the distinction between compensation eligibility and institutional accountability explained?
A decision about eligibility for a particular form of assistance does not necessarily resolve whether an incident occurred or whether a separate institution acted improperly.

It would be improper to describe the letter as a judicial admission of conspiracy. It would be equally improper to describe it as a judicial determination that the underlying allegations were false.

The distinction does not diminish its evidentiary importance.

NSW Trustee and Guardian Act 2009⁠.
The investigation should identify:

474. The central accountability problem: who owned the unresolved matter?
The most important question arising from this chronology is not simply how many institutions issued letters.
It is whether any institution accepted responsibility for examining the substance of the allegations and ensuring that matters outside its jurisdiction were directed to an appropriate body.
The investigation must identify, for every closure or referral:
	•	what issue was actually decided;
	•	what issue was left undecided;
	•	who was responsible for the undecided issue;
	•	whether the matter was referred;
	•	whether the referral was accepted;
	•	whether the affected person was informed;
	•	whether an effective review mechanism existed;
	•	whether the underlying risk or alleged harm was addressed.
If several bodies each dealt with a limited aspect of a complaint, the result may be an accountability gap even without a coordinated agreement between them.
If records show that institutions knowingly used jurisdictional boundaries to prevent a matter from being examined, that would raise a more serious question requiring investigation.
If records show that a complaint was repeatedly redirected without any receiving institution accepting responsibility, that may support a finding of systemic administrative failure.
If records show that the redirection was deliberately arranged to obstruct investigation, the evidence may support a different and more serious inference.
The evidence must decide which explanation is justified.
475. Conclusion of Part XXIX
The institutional decision chain is now defined as a central object of investigation.
The archive contains records from several institutions, but the existence of those records is only the beginning. The next task is to obtain the complete files behind the decisions and reconstruct the movement of information, authority and responsibility.
The critical distinction is between:
	•	a complaint being received;
	•	a complaint being assessed;
	•	a complaint being investigated;
	•	a complaint being referred;
	•	a complaint being resolved;
	•	and the person affected receiving an effective remedy.
Those are not interchangeable events.
The historical record must not allow an acknowledgment to be represented as an investigation, a jurisdictional refusal as an exoneration, or an administrative closure as proof that the underlying harm never occurred.
Nor should a sequence of institutional decisions be declared a criminal conspiracy without evidence of the required agreement and intention.
The institutional record must be examined as a whole, but every actor must remain individually accountable for the decisions they made, the information they possessed and the responsibilities they exercised or failed to exercise.
Next: PART XXX — THE CONTRADICTIONS, DISCREPANCIES AND OFFICIAL-RECORD INTEGRITY EXAMINATION.
This will examine conflicting descriptions, apparent inconsistencies, missing records, document provenance, source misclassification, chronology conflicts, unexplained changes in institutional reasoning and the distinction between an administrative error and deliberate falsification.


THE WHISTLEBLOWER, THE WITNESS AND THE STATE
PART XXX — THE CONTRADICTIONS, DISCREPANCIES AND OFFICIAL-RECORD INTEGRITY EXAMINATION
Conflicting accounts, apparent inconsistencies, missing records, document provenance, source misclassification, chronology conflicts, unexplained changes in institutional reasoning and the distinction between administrative error and deliberate falsification.
476. Purpose and evidentiary importance
This part examines a fundamental question:
Do the official records accurately and consistently represent the events, decisions, communications and institutional responsibilities they purport to document?
An investigation cannot simply collect documents and assume that their contents are accurate. Official records are important evidence, but they must still be examined for authenticity, completeness, internal consistency, accuracy, context and reliability.
A document may be authentic yet contain an error.
A document may accurately record what an official believed without accurately describing what happened.
A document may omit information that was available to the decision-maker.
A later institutional account may differ from an earlier contemporaneous record.
An administrative decision may rely on an inaccurate description that originated elsewhere.
And, in sufficiently serious circumstances, a discrepancy may raise the question of deliberate alteration, suppression or falsification.
These possibilities must be distinguished.
The investigation must neither dismiss discrepancies as harmless nor automatically interpret every discrepancy as evidence of deliberate wrongdoing.
A contradiction is an evidentiary issue. Its cause must be established.
477. The difference between a document, its contents and the event it describes
Every document should be examined at three separate levels.
Level 1 — The document itself
Questions include:
	•	Does the document exist?
	•	Is it complete?
	•	Is it an original, copy, scan, export or reconstruction?
	•	Who created or issued it?
	•	When was it created?
	•	Has it been modified?
	•	Is its provenance established?
Level 2 — The recorded statement
Questions include:
	•	What does the document actually say?
	•	Who supplied the information?
	•	Is the statement attributed to a particular person?
	•	Does it record a direct observation, a report from another person, an opinion or an assumption?
	•	Does it distinguish fact from allegation?
	•	Does it identify the source of the information?
Level 3 — The underlying event
Questions include:
	•	Did the event occur?
	•	Is the recorded description accurate?
	•	Are there independent records?
	•	Are there witnesses?
	•	Does other contemporaneous evidence corroborate or contradict it?
	•	Was the information later relied upon in a decision?
This three-level approach prevents a common evidentiary error: treating the existence of a document as automatic proof of every assertion contained within it.
It also prevents the opposite error: dismissing a document merely because its contents have not yet been independently corroborated.
An authentic official record is evidence that the record was created and that the identified information was recorded. Its weight in proving the underlying event depends on the circumstances of creation, the author’s knowledge, the source of the information and the available corroboration.

The following register identifies material discrepancies and verification tasks already apparent from the documentary history.
Reference	Discrepancy or issue	Required examination
