479. D01 — The 18 November 2021 PID filename and institutional identity
The archive contains a document whose filename describes it as an IBAC PID rejection.
However, the document itself identifies the Commonwealth Ombudsman’s Public Interest Disclosure Team and refers to PID-2021-400008-R.
Source: 18 November 2021 PID review⁠.
This is a demonstrable source-identification discrepancy between the filename and the contents.
The correct treatment is to identify the institution from the original document, not to repeat the filename as though it establishes authorship.
The investigation should record:
	•	the original filename;
	•	the document’s actual heading and letterhead;
	•	the author’s name and position;
	•	the reference number;
	•	the date;
	•	the statutory framework identified;
	•	the recipient;
	•	the source from which the document was obtained;
	•	whether the filename was assigned before or after archival.
The discrepancy matters because institutional identity determines jurisdiction, statutory authority and the correct interpretation of the decision.
It also demonstrates why an archive must not rely solely on filenames.
Preliminary finding: the filename is not a reliable substitute for the document’s institutional identity. The document’s contents identify the Commonwealth Ombudsman as the institution involved.
Classification: Documented discrepancy, subject to final verification against the original file.
There is no present basis for calling the filename discrepancy deliberate falsification.
480. D02 — Federal Court correspondence and the DSS employment issue
The Federal Court General Counsel letter dated 27 March 2023 raises a more substantive question.
Source: Federal Court PID assessment — 27 March 2023⁠.
The archive’s analysis identifies information concerning DSS employment alongside a later conclusion that the disclosure was not established as having been made by a public official.
The relevant question is not whether the two statements appear inconsistent when isolated from context.
The question is whether the decision-maker correctly applied the relevant statutory definition to the employment facts and the circumstances of the disclosure.
The investigation must obtain:
	•	The original employment records.
	•	The precise information about employment supplied to the Federal Court.
	•	The applicable statutory definition at the relevant date.
	•	The complete assessment and reasons.
	•	Any internal advice concerning the definition.
	•	Any enquiry made to DSS or another Commonwealth body.
	•	Any record explaining why the employment information was considered insufficient.
Several explanations remain possible.
The employment relationship may not have satisfied the statutory definition in the relevant circumstances. The information may have been incomplete. The decision-maker may have applied an incorrect interpretation. The assessment may have overlooked relevant material. Or the correspondence may contain an unexplained inconsistency.
The investigation must determine which explanation is supported.
It would be premature to label the matter deliberate falsification. It would also be inadequate to ignore the discrepancy simply because the decision came from an official legal office.
Preliminary finding: a material question exists about the relationship between the recorded employment information and the conclusion concerning public-official status.
Classification: Apparent documentary inconsistency requiring primary-source verification and statutory analysis.
481. D03 — The 18 June 2023 non-allocation notification
Source: 18 June 2023 notification⁠.
The archive identifies this document as a notification of a decision not to allocate a disclosure.
Its relationship to the 27 March 2023 Federal Court letter must not be assumed.
The document should be examined to establish:
	•	the issuing institution;
	•	the responsible officer;
	•	the relevant statutory provision;
	•	the disclosure reference;
	•	whether it concerns the same disclosure;
	•	whether the decision followed a review or reassessment;
	•	whether new material had been submitted;
	•	whether the decision relied on earlier findings;
	•	whether any alternative investigative body was identified.
The date is important because it may indicate a later stage in the handling of the disclosure. But chronology alone does not establish that the two decisions were coordinated.
The critical question is whether the June notification represents a separate decision, a continuation of the earlier process, a communication from another body or an administrative record of an action already taken.
Preliminary finding: the existence of the separate notification is documented in the archive; its issuer, statutory basis and relationship to earlier correspondence require confirmation.
Classification: Official-record identification with unresolved provenance and procedural relationship.
482. D04 — Commonwealth Ombudsman service restriction: original document versus archive cover
Source: Commonwealth Ombudsman service restriction — 8 August 2025⁠.
The archive description indicates that the first page is an author-created cover and the second page contains official letterhead.
This distinction is essential.
An archive cover may summarise, contextualise or classify an official document. It must not be represented as part of the original correspondence unless it was actually issued by the institution.
The investigation should preserve the cover and official letter as separate evidentiary objects.
It should also obtain the complete official correspondence, including all pages and attachments, and establish:
	•	the exact restriction imposed;
	•	the date it took effect;
	•	its duration;
	•	the conduct relied upon;
	•	the legal or policy basis;
	•	the responsible decision-maker;
	•	any exceptions;
	•	review or reconsideration rights;
	•	subsequent amendments or extensions.
The restriction should then be assessed against the contemporaneous complaints and communications.
The relevant question is whether it was a properly reasoned and proportionate administrative response, or whether the evidence indicates an improper purpose or effect.
The fact that the restriction followed earlier complaints is relevant chronology, but not sufficient proof of retaliation.
Preliminary finding: the distinction between author-created archive material and official correspondence must be maintained. The operative terms require full examination.
Classification: Source-integrity issue and incomplete examination of an official decision.
483. D05 — Archive totals and inconsistent document counts
The archive has contained different document counts across different dates, repositories and inventory methods.
The historical inventories identified in the preceding parts include:
	•	a 4 October 2026 README reporting 5,583 files, including 2,840 PDFs;
	•	a 19 September 2026 Backup inventory reporting 545 blobs, including 531 PDFs;
	•	a 20 September 2026 government-evidence path reporting 138 PDFs;
	•	an earlier reference to 186 PDFs in Backup;
	•	a later folder inventory referring to 95 PDFs;
	•	additional official Drive and Gmail PDFs copied into a presentation repository.
These numbers must not be added together or presented as though they represent one simultaneous inventory.
They refer to different dates, repositories, paths and potentially different counting methods.
The correct forensic method is to establish:
	•	The repository and branch examined.
	•	The commit or snapshot date.
	•	Whether the count includes folders, files, blobs or unique documents.
	•	Whether duplicate copies are included.
	•	Whether generated files and derived documents are included.
	•	Whether deleted or superseded files are counted.
	•	Whether submodules or external links are included.
	•	Whether the inventory was generated automatically or manually.
The public repositories provide a basis for independent examination:
	•	Primary archive⁠
	•	Backup repository⁠
	•	Archive data documents index⁠
	•	Archive timeline data⁠
A reliable inventory should provide a dated manifest with one row per file, including repository, path, filename, file size, hash, format, source classification and duplicate status.
Preliminary finding: the different counts cannot responsibly be treated as contradictory until their scope and dates are normalised.
Classification: Inventory discrepancy requiring scope reconciliation.
484. D06 — Werribee Mercy incident report IR8415987
Source: Werribee Mercy incident report IR8415987⁠.
The archive filename describes the record as a report of fatal injury in which a provider participant was revived.
That filename is not a substitute for examining the report itself.
The original record must be inspected to establish:
	•	the incident date and time;
	•	the person who created the report;
	•	the incident classification;
	•	the description of the injury or medical event;
	•	the clinical observations recorded;
	•	any treatment or resuscitation described;
	•	the people notified;
	•	the investigation undertaken;
	•	the final incident outcome;
	•	any corrections or subsequent entries.
The investigation should distinguish clinical records from incident-management records.
A hospital incident report may document a reported event, internal classification or administrative response. It may not contain all clinical evidence needed to establish the precise medical circumstances.
The relevant supporting material may include clinical notes, emergency response records, medication records, observation charts, discharge documentation, investigation reports and any independent review.
The report should not be described as proving every detail of a fatal injury or revival until the complete record has been examined.
At the same time, a filename that refers to a serious incident is a legitimate reason to obtain and preserve the original record and associated clinical documentation.
Preliminary finding: the existence of the archive item is documented; its substantive medical and incident-management contents require direct examination.
Classification: Official-record lead; underlying event details not independently established by the filename.
485. D07 — Different institutions, different decisions, one broader chronology
A further discrepancy can arise when separate institutions describe the same broad history using different classifications.
One may describe an issue as a public-interest disclosure. Another may describe it as a complaint about service delivery. Another may treat it as a guardianship matter, an FOI request, a compensation issue or a jurisdictional matter.
Those classifications may all be technically correct within their limited statutory contexts.
But the use of different classifications can also fragment the historical record.
For example, a complaint concerning an incident may contain several distinct allegations:
	•	the original event;
	•	the conduct of a provider;
	•	the conduct of a public official;
	•	the adequacy of an investigation;
	•	the accuracy of a subsequent record;
	•	the response to a protected disclosure;
	•	the consequences of an administrative decision.
If an institution considers only one of those issues, its closure cannot automatically be represented as a resolution of the entire matter.
The investigation should therefore compare each institution’s description of the matter against the original complaint.
A master issue register should record:
Issue	Original allegation	Institution’s classification	What was decided	What remained unresolved
Original incident	To be extracted from primary complaint	To be verified	Not assumed	To be identified
Provider conduct	To be extracted	To be verified	Not assumed	To be identified
Public-official conduct	To be extracted	To be verified	Not assumed	To be identified
Complaint handling	To be extracted	To be verified	Not assumed	To be identified
Record accuracy	To be extracted	To be verified	Not assumed	To be identified
Reprisal or detriment	To be extracted	To be verified	Not assumed	To be identified
The purpose is to prevent one institution’s limited decision from being used to imply that every component of a wider complaint was examined.
486. D08 — Repetition of disputed information across institutions
One of the most important forensic questions concerns the movement of information.
A statement may originate in one record and later appear in several other documents. The later documents may then appear to provide independent confirmation, even though they all derive from the same original source.
This is a form of evidentiary dependence.
For example:
	•	Institution A records an allegation.
	•	Institution B receives Institution A’s summary.
	•	Institution C relies on Institution B’s correspondence.
	•	Institution D later refers to the same description as an established historical fact.
Four documents may then repeat one original assertion.
That is not necessarily four independent sources.
The investigation must identify the first known source of each material statement and trace every later repetition.
For each repeated assertion, record:
	•	Original author.
	•	Original date.
	•	Original source of information.
	•	Whether the statement was firsthand or hearsay.
	•	Every subsequent recipient.
	•	Every later document that repeats it.
	•	Whether recipients independently verified it.
	•	Whether corrections or objections were supplied.
	•	Whether the statement influenced any decision.
This is particularly important where a disputed classification, risk description or allegation may affect access to services, credibility, complaint handling or administrative decision-making.
A repeated error can become institutionally entrenched without anyone deliberately coordinating its repetition.
Alternatively, evidence that an actor knowingly propagated information after being advised that it was false may raise a more serious question.
The investigation must establish the chain.
487. D09 — Chronology conflicts and the importance of date classification
A chronology is only reliable if its dates are correctly classified.
A document may contain several different dates:
	•	date of the event;
	•	date the event was reported;
	•	date the document was created;
	•	date it was signed;
	•	date it was sent;
	•	date it was received;
	•	date it was registered;
	•	date a decision was made;
	•	date the decision was communicated;
	•	date the document was uploaded to an archive.
These dates must not be treated as interchangeable.
A letter created on one date may have been received several days later. A complaint may describe an earlier event. A decision may be dated before it was communicated. A file may be uploaded to GitHub long after it was created.
A master chronology should therefore contain separate fields for each relevant date.
Where dates conflict, the investigation should preserve both entries and identify the source of each.
It should not silently select the date that best supports a preferred narrative.
A chronology conflict may reveal nothing more than an ordinary administrative delay. It may also expose a mistaken decision date, retrospective record entry, incomplete file or inaccurate account of events.
The date itself is evidence, but its meaning depends on what the date represents.
488. D10 — Archive descriptions must not become substitute findings
The archive contains official documents, summaries, indexes, descriptions, reports and analytical material.
These categories must be kept distinct.
An archive description may be written by the document’s owner, a researcher or an automated system. It can assist navigation but does not become an official institutional finding merely because it appears beside an official PDF.
Every archive entry should identify:
	•	original document title;
	•	original issuing body;
	•	original author or signatory, where available;
	•	original date;
	•	reference number;
	•	document type;
	•	source location;
	•	archive filename;
	•	whether the file is original or derived;
	•	whether the description is an official title or an archive-created description;
	•	whether the contents have been examined.
The official register should make clear whether a statement is:
A. Original official wording: text appearing in the official document.
B. Archive metadata: information used to identify and organise the file.
C. Researcher summary: a description of the document’s contents.
D. Author allegation: an assertion made by the complainant or author.
E. Analytical inference: a conclusion drawn from multiple records.
F. Established finding: a conclusion reached by a body with the relevant authority, or a carefully defined historical finding supported by the evidence.
This separation protects the integrity of the archive and the credibility of its conclusions.
489. Administrative error, negligence, maladministration and deliberate falsification
A discrepancy can have different causes and different legal consequences.
The following distinctions should be maintained.
Administrative error
An incorrect date, filename, reference number, classification or transcription may arise without deliberate intent.
The error should be corrected transparently, with the original version preserved.
Negligence or inadequate recordkeeping
An institution may fail to create, retain, verify or correct records to the standard reasonably required by its responsibilities.
The relevant legal duties and consequences depend on the circumstances.
Maladministration
A decision or administrative process may be unreasonable, procedurally unfair, inadequately explained, based on irrelevant considerations or otherwise inconsistent with proper public administration.
The precise legal or statutory meaning depends on the relevant jurisdiction and context.
Misrepresentation
A record or communication may present information inaccurately or in a misleading manner. The investigation must determine whether this arose from mistake, omission, misunderstanding or intentional conduct.
Deliberate alteration or falsification
A person may knowingly create, alter, suppress or misrepresent a record for an improper purpose.
That is a serious allegation and requires evidence identifying the record, the alteration or false statement, the person responsible, the relevant knowledge and intention, and the applicable legal provisions.
These categories must not be treated as synonyms.
A mistake is not automatically corruption. A serious administrative failure is not automatically a criminal offence. But deliberate falsification must not be disguised as an ordinary clerical error where the evidence establishes intentional conduct.
490. The forensic examination of original documents
The following procedures should be applied to every material document.
A. Provenance
Establish where the document came from, who supplied it, how it was obtained and whether the chain of custody is documented.
B. Authenticity
Compare the document with an original institutional copy, an authenticated electronic record or another reliable source.
C. Completeness
Check page numbering, attachments, schedules, referenced enclosures, missing pages and unexplained gaps.
D. Metadata
Where available, examine creation dates, modification dates, author fields, email headers, document properties and system audit information.
E. Internal consistency
Compare the document’s dates, references, names, statutory provisions, factual assertions and reasoning.
F. External consistency
Compare the document with contemporaneous correspondence, other official records, witness accounts and independent evidence.
G. Version comparison
Where several versions exist, compare them to identify additions, deletions, changes in wording, altered dates or changed conclusions.
H. Preservation
Retain the original file unchanged. Any OCR, conversion, redaction, annotation or extraction should create a separate derivative copy.
A SHA-256 hash can help verify that a file has remained unchanged since a particular hash was calculated. It cannot establish that the document was authentic before it entered the archive.
A digital timestamp may establish that a particular data object existed no later than a particular time. It cannot independently establish the truth of the contents or the identity of the person who created it.
491. The source-of-assertion examination
Every important factual assertion should be traceable to its source.
The following questions should be asked:
	•	Who first made the assertion?
	•	Was it based on personal observation?
	•	Was it based on information supplied by another person?
	•	Was the original source identified?
	•	Was the assertion recorded contemporaneously?
	•	Was it subsequently disputed?
	•	Was contrary evidence supplied?
	•	Did the institution investigate the dispute?
	•	Was the assertion repeated without verification?
	•	Did it influence a later decision?
The importance of this examination cannot be overstated.
If an institution repeatedly relies upon a statement that originated from an unverified allegation, the repetition does not transform that allegation into an established fact.
If an institution receives credible contrary information, it should be possible to identify whether the contradiction was considered and how it affected the decision.
A record that contains only one side of a disputed history may be incomplete even if every sentence in it is accurately transcribed.
492. The suppression and missing-record examination
Missing records require careful treatment.
A missing document does not automatically prove suppression. It may have been:
	•	never created;
	•	created but not retained;
	•	stored under another reference;
	•	misfiled;
	•	transferred to another custodian;
	•	deleted under a lawful retention process;
	•	lost through a technical failure;
	•	withheld under a lawful exemption;
	•	omitted from an incomplete search.
The investigation should establish which explanation applies.
Where a document is referred to in correspondence but is absent from the supplied file, the investigator should request:
	•	the document itself;
	•	its creation and registration details;
	•	the identity of its custodian;
	•	its storage location;
	•	any transfer record;
	•	any deletion or destruction record;
	•	the applicable retention schedule;
	•	the search steps undertaken;
	•	the reasons for any withholding.
A statement that an institution could not locate a record is not proof that the event never happened.
Equally, the absence of a record does not prove that the institution deliberately destroyed it.
The investigation should record the missing item, the evidence that it once existed or was expected to exist, and the steps taken to locate it.
493. The contradictory-reasons examination
A particularly important category of discrepancy occurs when an institution gives different reasons for the same decision over time.
For example, a decision may initially be described as jurisdictional, later as a resource issue, and subsequently as a decision based on the merits.
Such changes may have legitimate explanations. Additional information may have emerged, a review may have corrected an earlier explanation, or different staff may have described separate stages of the process.
But the change must be documented.
The investigation should compare:
	•	the first explanation;
	•	the formal written reasons;
	•	later correspondence;
	•	internal decision records;
	•	any review outcome;
	•	any explanation supplied to another institution.
The key question is whether the later explanation is consistent with the original decision and the contemporaneous evidence.
A material change in reasons without explanation may raise concerns about procedural fairness, decision integrity or the reliability of the institutional account.
If records show that the original reasons were knowingly false, the issue becomes substantially more serious.
494. Contradiction does not mean equivalence
When two documents conflict, both cannot necessarily be correct in the same respect.
The investigator must not automatically treat competing accounts as equally reliable.
Reliability should be assessed using:
	•	proximity to the event;
	•	firsthand knowledge;
	•	contemporaneous recording;
	•	consistency with independent records;
	•	internal coherence;
	•	accuracy of the author’s role and knowledge;
	•	whether the author had a reason to misstate the facts;
	•	whether corrections were made;
	•	whether the record was created for an operational, legal or administrative purpose.
A contemporaneous record may carry significant weight, but it is not infallible.
A later account may contain information unavailable at the time, but it must be examined for its source and reliability.
The correct approach is to explain why one account is better supported, rather than merely listing the contradiction and refusing to assess it.
495. The official-record integrity matrix
Every material record should receive a structured integrity assessment.
Field	Required entry
Document ID	Unique archive identifier
Official title	Exact title on the original
Issuing institution	Confirmed from the document
Author/signatory	Name and position, where available
Date	Original date and relevant event dates
Reference	Official reference number
Provenance	Source and acquisition history
Completeness	Full, partial or unknown
Authenticity	Verified, probable, disputed or unverified
Metadata	Available creation and modification information
Internal consistency	Any apparent contradictions
External consistency	Corroborating or conflicting sources
Derivative status	Original, scan, OCR, copy or summary
Evidentiary value	What the document directly establishes
Limitations	What it does not establish
Outstanding action	Record or clarification required
This matrix should become part of the public-facing documentary register.
It will allow a researcher, journalist, lawyer, oversight body or other reader to understand not only what a document is, but how much weight can responsibly be placed upon it.
496. Findings arising from the discrepancy examination
The material presently identified supports the following preliminary findings.
Finding 1 — Source-identification discrepancies exist.
The November 2021 PID filename does not accurately identify the institution named in the document itself. This demonstrates the need to prioritise original document contents over archive filenames.
Finding 2 — A material statutory-assessment question exists in the Federal Court correspondence.
The relationship between the DSS employment information and the public-official conclusion requires comparison with the original employment evidence and the applicable statutory definition.
Finding 3 — The June 2023 non-allocation notification requires provenance verification.
Its issuing institution and relationship to the earlier Federal Court assessment must be established before it can be used to draw conclusions about institutional continuity.
Finding 4 — The Commonwealth Ombudsman restriction record requires separation of archive-created material from official correspondence.
The full operative decision, reasons, duration and review rights must be examined.
Finding 5 — Different archive totals require reconciliation.
The counts represent different dates and scopes and must not be combined into a single total without a common inventory method.
Finding 6 — The Werribee Mercy incident report must be assessed from its original contents.
The filename is an investigative lead, not a substitute for the complete incident and clinical record.
Finding 7 — Repeated institutional descriptions require source tracing.
An assertion repeated across several records may still derive from a single original source. Independent corroboration must be distinguished from repetition.
Finding 8 — Missing records and changed explanations require investigation.
Their existence may indicate ordinary administrative problems or more serious conduct. The cause must be established through custodial and metadata evidence.
497. What can be said about deliberate falsification?
At this stage, the identified discrepancies do not collectively establish deliberate falsification by any named person or institution.
That is not a declaration that deliberate falsification did not occur.
It means that the evidence presently described establishes identifiable inconsistencies and verification requirements, but does not yet establish the responsible person, intentional act, knowledge, purpose and applicable legal elements necessary for such a conclusion.
The investigation should specifically test whether any person:
	•	knowingly entered false information;
	•	altered an official record without authority;
	•	concealed a material correction;
	•	knowingly presented an allegation as an established fact;
	•	removed or withheld relevant information for an improper purpose;
	•	misrepresented the existence or contents of a document;
	•	knowingly supplied false information to another decision-maker;
	•	destroyed or concealed records to obstruct an investigation.
If the records support any of these possibilities, the investigation should identify the specific evidence and the appropriate legal or integrity pathway.
A conclusion of deliberate falsification must be supported by more than an unexplained discrepancy. But an institution should not be permitted to close the question merely by labelling every inconsistency an administrative error.
498. Required documentary actions
The following actions should be prioritised.
	•	Obtain the complete original Federal Court PID assessment file.
	•	Obtain the employment records relevant to the DSS public-official issue.
	•	Confirm the issuing institution and statutory basis of the 18 June 2023 notification.
	•	Obtain the complete Commonwealth Ombudsman service-restriction decision.
	•	Preserve the original 18 November 2021 PID review and correct the archive metadata.
	•	Obtain the full Werribee Mercy IR8415987 report and associated records.
	•	Reconcile repository inventories against dated Git commits.
	•	Create a SHA-256 manifest for all material primary documents.
	•	Identify duplicate records and distinguish them from independent sources.
	•	Trace the origin of material assertions repeated across institutional correspondence.
	•	Identify missing attachments and referenced records.
	•	Compare original and later versions of decisions and correspondence.
	•	Record every discrepancy in a version-controlled register.
	•	Obtain search and retention explanations for material records that cannot be located.
	•	Preserve all corrections without overwriting the original historical record.
499. Final conclusion of Part XXX
The discrepancy examination demonstrates why a documentary archive must be treated as an evidentiary system rather than a collection of files.
A filename can be wrong while the document is authentic.
A document can be authentic while its contents are inaccurate.
A decision can be official while its reasoning remains open to scrutiny.
An institution can accurately record its own decision while leaving the underlying allegation unresolved.
A repeated statement can appear to have multiple sources while deriving from one original assertion.
A missing document can indicate a routine recordkeeping problem or something more serious.
The difference can only be established by preserving the originals, tracing provenance, examining metadata, comparing versions and obtaining the complete institutional files.
The discrepancies identified here are not to be erased, minimised or silently corrected. They must remain visible in the historical record, together with the evidence that resolves them.
The integrity of the archive depends not on every document being perfect, but on every document being examined honestly, every correction being transparent and every material contradiction being preserved until it is resolved.
PART XXXI — THE INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION AND ACCOUNTABILITY FRAMEWORK
How the documentary record can be converted into an actionable investigation: preservation orders, independent oversight, witness examination, institutional accountability, findings, remedies and restitution.
500. The transition from documentary examination to independent investigation
The preceding parts have established a documentary framework covering:
	•	the institutional chronology;
	•	public-interest disclosures;
	•	administrative and jurisdictional decisions;
	•	alleged institutional coordination;
	•	the movement of information between bodies;
	•	documentary contradictions;
	•	archive integrity;
	•	unresolved evidentiary questions;
	•	potential accountability pathways.
The next stage is to convert that material into a structured independent investigation.
The investigation should not begin by requiring the complainant to prove every institutional interaction without access to the records held by those institutions.
Nor should it begin by assuming that every adverse decision was unlawful.
It should begin with preservation of the evidence, identification of the responsible custodians, disclosure of the decision-making records and independent assessment of the unresolved issues.
The purpose is to establish what happened, who was responsible, what legal or administrative duties applied, what harm resulted and what remedy is required.
501. Independence: the essential requirement
An investigation cannot provide meaningful accountability if the body examining the allegations is materially implicated in the events under examination.
Independence requires more than a different staff member reading the same file.
The investigator should have:
	•	no material involvement in the original decisions;
	•	no personal or institutional conflict of interest;
	•	authority to obtain relevant records;
	•	access to witnesses;
	•	authority to examine the conduct of all relevant actors within the investigation’s jurisdiction;
	•	appropriate safeguards for confidential and sensitive information;
	•	the ability to make findings without direction from the institutions being examined;
	•	a transparent process for identifying and addressing conflicts.
Where the allegations concern several jurisdictions, the investigation should identify which body has authority over each component.
A Commonwealth integrity investigation cannot automatically determine every state matter. A state integrity body cannot automatically determine every Commonwealth matter. Private service-provider conduct may require a different statutory pathway.
The investigation should not allow these divisions to become a reason for the complete matter to disappear between institutions.
502. Terms of reference
The following terms of reference are proposed.
Term 1 — Establish the factual chronology
Determine the dates, events, decisions, communications and consequences relevant to the complaints and disclosures.
Term 2 — Examine the original incident and subsequent records
Obtain and assess the original records concerning the serious incident described in the archive, including relevant incident-management and clinical material.
Term 3 — Examine public-interest disclosures
Determine what information was disclosed, to whom, under what statutory framework and how each disclosure was assessed.
Term 4 — Examine the accuracy of institutional decisions
Assess whether decisions were based on accurate information, relevant considerations, lawful authority and fair procedures.
Term 5 — Examine inter-agency communications
Determine what communications, referrals, information exchanges and instructions occurred between relevant institutions and individuals.
Term 6 — Examine possible reprisal
Determine whether any adverse action was connected to a disclosure, complaint or other protected activity, and whether the relevant legal requirements are satisfied.
Term 7 — Examine alleged coordination
Determine whether the evidence supports independent action, lawful coordination, systemic failure, improper cooperation or an agreement to pursue unlawful conduct.
Term 8 — Examine record integrity
Determine whether material records were incomplete, inaccurate, altered, suppressed, destroyed or misrepresented.
Term 9 — Examine financial and property administration
Determine whether relevant financial and property decisions were authorised, properly reasoned, documented and accounted for.
Term 10 — Examine disability and support administration
Determine whether relevant decisions and service-delivery practices complied with applicable statutory duties and support obligations.
Term 11 — Examine institutional complaint handling
Determine whether each institution properly identified its jurisdiction, assessed the substance of the allegations and referred unresolved matters appropriately.
Term 12 — Determine harm and remedy
Identify the consequences of any established conduct and recommend appropriate correction, restoration, compensation, accountability or other remedy within the investigator’s authority.
503. Preservation notices and immediate evidence protection
The first practical step should be preservation of relevant records.
The investigation should identify the likely custodians and issue appropriate preservation requests or notices under the available legal powers.
The records should include:
	•	original complaints and disclosures;
	•	all attachments;
	•	email and messaging records;
	•	internal memoranda;
	•	decision drafts;
	•	case-management notes;
	•	call logs and telephone notes;
	•	meeting records;
	•	referral records;
	•	records of information disclosure;
	•	document access logs;
	•	metadata and audit trails;
	•	delegation and approval records;
	•	relevant financial records;
	•	service-delivery records;
	•	records concerning the creation, alteration or deletion of material documents.
The preservation process should cover both active and archived systems.
Where records are subject to routine deletion or system migration, the custodian should be asked to preserve relevant material before the ordinary retention process removes it.
Preservation must not be confused with a finding of wrongdoing. It is a precaution necessary to protect the evidence while the allegations are examined.
504. The witness examination framework
Witness interviews should be structured around what each person directly knows.
For every witness, the investigator should record:
	•	identity and relevant position;
	•	responsibilities at the relevant time;
	•	relationship to the events;
	•	documents created or received;
	•	direct observations;
	•	information received from others;
	•	communications with other actors;
	•	decisions made or implemented;
	•	reasons recorded;
	•	recollection and its limitations;
	•	any conflicts of interest;
	•	any documents that corroborate or contradict the account.
Witnesses should not be asked leading questions that assume the truth of disputed allegations.
They should be asked to identify the records on which their recollection is based.
A particularly important question is:
What did you know at the time you made or implemented this decision, and what document or communication establishes that knowledge?
This question can distinguish personal knowledge from later institutional summaries.
505. Priority witnesses and institutional custodians
The investigation should identify witnesses by function before assuming that any particular person is responsible.
Priority categories include:
	•	The original author or recipient of the first material complaint.
	•	The officers responsible for PID intake and assessment.
	•	The officials responsible for the Federal Court General Counsel assessment.
	•	The custodians of relevant DSS employment records.
	•	The officers responsible for the Commonwealth Ombudsman service restriction.
	•	The officials responsible for the LECC jurisdictional assessment.
	•	The NSW Trustee decision-makers and financial record custodians.
	•	The relevant NDIS decision-makers and Commission complaint handlers.
	•	The custodians of the Werribee Mercy incident and clinical records.
	•	The people responsible for any referral between institutions.
	•	Any individual who created, altered, approved or relied upon disputed records.
This list identifies functions and records to be examined. It does not assert that the individuals occupying those roles engaged in wrongdoing.
506. The investigative question matrix
Investigation question	Evidence required	Intended outcome
What happened in the original incident?	Original incident and clinical records, witnesses, contemporaneous documents	Factual chronology
What was disclosed?	Original complaints, attachments, correspondence	Accurate disclosure history
What did each institution assess?	Complete case files and decisions	Scope of each assessment
Who made each decision?	Delegations, approvals and file notes	Individual responsibility
What communications occurred?	Emails, messages, calls, meeting records	Communication chronology
Was information accurate?	Original sources and later copies	Information reliability
Was there retaliation?	Disclosure dates, adverse actions, reasons and communications	Causation and legal assessment
Was there coordination?	Evidence of agreement, common instructions and knowledge	Coordination finding
Were records altered or suppressed?	Original versions, metadata and audit logs	Record-integrity finding
Was financial administration proper?	Decisions, statements, valuations and accounting	Financial accountability
Were supports delivered?	Plans, agreements, invoices and service records	Service-delivery finding
Was an effective remedy available?	Complaint outcomes, review rights and referrals	Remedy assessment
507. Findings must be specific and attributed
An independent report should not conclude merely that an institution failed or that the complainant was wrong.
It should make findings about identifiable acts and omissions.
Each finding should specify:
	•	the relevant event;
	•	the date or period;
	•	the person or institution responsible;
	•	the evidence relied upon;
	•	the applicable duty or standard;
	•	any conflicting evidence;
	•	the reasoning;
	•	the level of certainty;
	•	the consequences;
	•	the recommended remedy.
The report should also distinguish between an individual error and an institutional failure.
An employee may make a mistake that is corrected promptly. An institution may have systemic procedures that repeatedly produce the same error. A decision-maker may knowingly act contrary to the evidence. Those are materially different findings.
508. Proposed finding classifications
The following classifications should be used consistently throughout the final investigation.
	•	Established: supported by sufficiently reliable evidence for the stated purpose.
	•	Documented: the record exists and establishes the fact of its creation or recorded contents.
	•	Officially acknowledged: an institution has formally recognised receipt, an event, a decision or another specified matter.
	•	Corroborated: supported by independent sources.
	•	Partially corroborated: supported in part, with material details unresolved.
	•	Contradicted: inconsistent with reliable evidence.
	•	Unsupported: the available evidence does not presently substantiate the assertion.
	•	Not determined: the evidence is insufficient to reach a conclusion.
	•	Disproved: reliable evidence affirmatively establishes that the relevant proposition is false.
	•	Referred for further investigation: the evidence raises a serious issue requiring examination by a body with appropriate powers.
These classifications should not be used interchangeably.
In particular, unsupported does not necessarily mean disproved, and not determined does not mean false.
Likewise, an official acknowledgment does not automatically establish the truth of the allegations acknowledged.
509. Proposed final investigation report structure
The independent investigation should produce a final report containing:
	•	Executive findings.
	•	Scope and terms of reference.
	•	Methodology and evidentiary standards.
	•	Background and relevant history.
	•	Complete chronology.
	•	Institutional decision-chain reconstruction.
	•	Examination of each primary document.
	•	Examination of the original incident.
	•	Public-interest disclosure history.
	•	Examination of institutional communications.
	•	Examination of alleged coordination and conspiracy.
	•	Examination of possible reprisal.
	•	Examination of record integrity.
	•	Financial and property administration.
	•	Disability and support administration.
	•	Witness evidence.
	•	Contradictions and alternative explanations.
	•	Findings against each relevant term of reference.
	•	Identified systemic failures.
	•	Individual and institutional accountability.
	•	Harm and consequences.
	•	Recommended remedies.
	•	Referral recommendations.
	•	Evidence register and appendices.
The report should include public links to accessible primary documents wherever possible, with precise references to page numbers, dates and relevant passages.
A public report should also distinguish material that cannot lawfully be published because of privacy, confidentiality, legal privilege or other applicable restrictions.
510. The principle of an effective remedy
An investigation that identifies wrongdoing but provides no meaningful remedy may leave the affected person in substantially the same position.
The remedy assessment should therefore examine the actual consequences of any established failure.
Potential remedies may include:
	•	correction of inaccurate records;
	•	written acknowledgment of established administrative errors;
	•	reconsideration of decisions made on inaccurate information;
	•	restoration of improperly withheld entitlements where legally available;
	•	proper accounting for property or financial transactions;
	•	restoration of access to complaint mechanisms;
	•	reconsideration of service-delivery decisions;
	•	independent review of risk classifications;
	•	appropriate protection against retaliation;
	•	referral for disciplinary or criminal investigation where warranted;
	•	compensation or other redress where a legal basis exists;
	•	systemic reforms to prevent recurrence.
The appropriate remedy depends on the established facts, legal duties, jurisdiction and available powers.
The objective is not merely to produce another letter. It is to correct established wrongs and prevent their repetition.
511. Conclusion of Part XXXI
The investigation framework must be capable of examining both individual decisions and institutional systems.
It must have access to original records, the authority to examine communications and the independence to reach conclusions that may be uncomfortable for the institutions involved.
The complainant should not be required to accept a series of jurisdictional closures as though they collectively answer every allegation.
Nor should institutions be condemned without examining their actual decisions, responsibilities and evidence.
The proper outcome is a documented, reasoned and independently scrutinised account of what occurred.
An effective investigation must follow the evidence wherever it leads, including where that evidence establishes institutional error, serious maladministration, improper coordination, deliberate wrongdoing or an allegation that cannot be substantiated.
The historical record must remain intact regardless of the outcome.
Preservation First. Examination Second. Conclusion Last.
